docs.title: Welcome to JeKa
docs.text: JeKa is a modern build tool for Java, designed to simplify and streamline your development experience. It reshapes Java application building for a generation of developers seeking lightweight, accessible, yet powerful solutions.

docs.title: Next-Gen Java Build Tool
docs.text:
Java is evolving to become more developer-friendly and cloud-native ready. Developers no longer want to deal with heavy tools, verbose XML configurations, or external DSLs. JeKa aligns with this vision by offering:

  • Simplicity at its Core: Configure with properties or pure Java—no XML, no DSL.
  • No Setup Hassle: Start building regular or cloud-native applications immediately, with minimal configuration and requirements.
  • Gradual Complexity: Handle advanced scenarios using intuitive mechanisms without unnecessary complexity.
  • DevOps Bridge: Implement complex pipeline logic with robust Java and share it across your teams.
  • Super-lightweight: JeKa consists of a single zero-dependency JAR under 2MB. Install and upgrade in a flash.

docs.title: Ready to explore?
docs.text:
The easiest way to get started is by using the IntelliJ Plugin. You don't need to install JeKa for that.

  1. Start a new project and play with the scaffolded example. You can have a brief look at the tutorial to get an idea of what you can do.

  2. You can create projects in the IDE using Project - Java App/Lib or Project - Spring Boot templates. They scaffold basic projects, providing code and build instructions in README.md files.

  3. Explore and experiment with examples.

Prefer the command line? Install the CLI, then follow the Quick Start.

Have fun!

docs.title: Standard Properties
docs.text: Property Name Default Value Description jeka.version The JeKa version to use. It will be fetched from the repository specified first in the jeka.repos.download property. Use jeka.version=. to force the use of the locally installed version. jeka.distrib.location The exact location (directory) to get the JeKa distribution. If set, jeka.version will be ignored. jeka.distrib.repo The repository to download the JeKa distribution from. If set, it prevails over jeka.repos.download for this download only. jeka.java.version The version of the JDK used to run JeKa and compile code located in jeka-src. Should be 21 or higher. jeka.java.distrib temurin The distribution of JDK to fetch when jeka.java.version is mentioned. jeka.repos.download mavenCentral Comma-separated string of repositories to fetch Maven dependencies. More details here. jeka.repos.publish Comma-separated string of repositories to publish Maven artifacts. More details here. jeka.program.build See here Command line to execute to build the application when execution files are absent. jeka.kbean.default Name or class name of the KBean to use as default (when none is specified). jeka.test.skip Skip tests when building projects or codebases. jeka.platform.os linux, windows or mac Provides the OS of the running machine. jeka.platform.arch x86 64-bit, AArch64 64-bit Provides the architecture of the running machine. maven.classifier.os linux, windows or osx Provides the OS of the running machine, using maven nomenclature. maven.classifier.arch aarch_64, x86_64 or x86 Provides the architecture of the running machine, using maven nomenclature.

docs.title: JDK Selection Rules
docs.text:
1. If JEKA_JDK_HOME is set, use this JDK.
  2. If jeka.java.version is specified:
    • Use JDK from jeka.jdk.[version] if available.
    • Otherwise, fetch JDK from local cache or download it.
  3. If no version is specified:
    • Use JDK from JAVA_HOME if set.
    • Otherwise, fetch JDK 21 from local cache or download it.

docs.title: How JeKa Reads Properties
docs.text:
JeKa reads properties in this order:

  • Command-line arguments (as -Dmy.prop=xxx).
  • Environment variables (my.prop or MY_PROP). The bash launcher only recognizes the exact my.prop name for the properties it reads itself (jeka.version, jeka.java.version, jeka.java.distrib, jeka.jdk.X, ...).
  • The jeka.properties file in the base directory.
  • The jeka.properties files in parent directories, up to the first directory without one.
  • The global.properties file in [JEKA_USER_HOME].

docs.title: 1. No XML no DSL
docs.text: Use properties for configuration and Java code for logic.

docs.title: 2. Unified Model for Plugins and Build Logic
docs.text: Whether writing custom build logic or creating a reusable plugin, you use the same simple Java model: KBeans. They are similar to JavaBeans.

docs.title: 3. Immediate Feedback
docs.text: JeKa compiles and runs your build logic on-the-fly. There is no "configuring" phase that takes several seconds before the build starts.

docs.title: 4. Highly Portable
docs.text: Builds run on any machine, even without Java installed.

docs.title: My organization prevents access to Maven Central. What can I do?
docs.text:
You can configure Maven repositories in a central place by editing the [USER HOME]/.jeka/global.properties file.

jeka.repos.download=https://my.company/repo

# You can specify username/password
jeka.repos.download.username=myName
jeka.repos.download.password=myPassw0rd!

# ... or specify Authorization header to avoid password in clear
jeka.repos.download.headers.Authorization=Basic hKXhhtggjREfg4P=

To fetch JeKa distributions, specify the jeka.distrib.location property, pointing to a folder. This property is better placed in the jeka.properties file, as it may vary from one project to another.

docs.title: My organization prevents downloading JDKs. What can I do?
docs.text:
You can specify a local location for each JDK version you are using as follows: 

jeka.jdk.11=/my/path/to/jdk11/home
jeka.jdk.17=/my/path/to/jdk17/home
...
This information can be stored in the project's jeka.properties file, in [USER HOME]/.jeka/global.properties, or passed as environment variables.

docs.title: I'm behind a proxy, how should I configure JeKa?
docs.text:
JeKa just leverages the standard Java mechanism to handle proxies. For example, you can:

  • Set the JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS environment variable to -Dhttps.proxyHost=my.proxy.host -Dhttps.proxyPort=8888.
  • Or specify proxy properties to the JeKa command line, such as: -Dhttps.proxyHost=my.proxy.host -Dhttps.proxyPort=8888.

See here for more details on arguments.

docs.title: How can I use Maven/Gradle in conjunction with JeKa?
docs.text:
Nothing prevents using JeKa alongside Maven or Gradle in the same project, except that in an IDE, synchronization may interfere between the two systems.

To avoid this, the jeka-src folder should exist in its own IntelliJ module. JeKa provides a simple way to achieve this.

From an existing Maven/Gradle project, execute: 

jeka base: scaffold
This will generate a jeka-src folder,along with a jeka.properties file.

Edit the jeka.properties file, and add: 

@intellij.splitModule=true
Generate the .iml file by synchronizing within the IDE, or by running: 
jeka intellij: sync
In IntelliJ, go to Project Settings -> Modules -> Import Module -> choose [project dir]/.idea/xxxx-jeka.iml.

docs.title: How can I migrate my project from Maven?
docs.text: Follow Migrate a Maven Project. The jeka maven: migrateDeps command translates the dependencies of the pom.xml file.

docs.title: How to cache downloaded dependencies in GitHub Actions?
docs.text:
JeKa caches downloaded dependencies (JDKs, JeKa distributions, Maven artifacts, Node.js executables, etc.) in a single directory at [USER HOME]/.jeka/cache.

When running as a GitHub Action, this directory is empty at the start of the build. We need to save/restore it in order to make it persist from one build to another.

For this, we can use the cache action as follows: 

    - name: Restore JeKa cache
      uses: actions/cache/restore@v4
      with:
        path: ~/.jeka/cache
        key: ${{ runner.os }}

    - name: Run some JeKa commands
      run: "./jeka project: pack ..."

    - name: Save JeKa cache
      uses: actions/cache/save@v4
      with:
        path: ~/.jeka/cache
        key: ${{ runner.os }}

docs.title: How do I configure projects from code?
docs.text:
If you want to configure a project programmatically, either within the project itself or to create a plugin, you should access the JkProject instance directly instead of using the ProjectKBean.

The ProjectKBean initializes the project and configures it with its own settings in its init method. After that, it should not be modified. If you change the ProjectKBean instance in your code, the underlying JkProject instance will already have been configured by the ProjectKBean, meaning your changes will have no effect.

import dev.jeka.core.api.project.JkProject;
import dev.jeka.core.api.testing.JkTestProcessor;
import dev.jeka.core.tool.JkPostInit;
import dev.jeka.core.tool.KBean;
import dev.jeka.core.tool.builtins.project.ProjectKBean;

public class Build extends KBean {

    @JkPostInit(required = true)
    private void postInit(ProjectKBean projectKBean) {
        JkProject project = projectKBean.project;
        project.test.processor.engineBehavior
                .setProgressDisplayer(JkTestProcessor.JkProgressStyle.STEP);
    }
}

docs.title: How can I use the Eclipse compiler in JeKa?
docs.text:
JeKa can use any JSR199 Java compiler to compile your Java code. Just set the compiler instance you need as follows:

import dev.jeka.core.api.project.JkProject;
import dev.jeka.core.tool.JkDep;
import dev.jeka.core.tool.JkPostInit;
import dev.jeka.core.tool.KBean;
import dev.jeka.core.tool.builtins.project.ProjectKBean;
import org.eclipse.jdt.internal.compiler.tool.EclipseCompiler;

@JkDep("org.eclipse.jdt:ecj:3.42.0")
public class Build extends KBean {

    @JkPostInit(required = true)
    private void postInit(ProjectKBean projectKBean) {
        JkProject project = projectKBean.project;
        project.compilerToolChain.setCompileTool(new EclipseCompiler());

        // You may pass additional options to the compiler
        project.compilation.addJavaCompilerOptions("-nowarn");
    }
}

docs.title: How can I sync Eclipse/IntelliJ without using ProjectKBean?
docs.text:
ProjectKBean and BaseKBean provide IDE synchronization out-of-the-box, but you may prefer not to use them.

If you use a different structure to build your project, simply let your KBean implement JkIdeSupportSupplier and implement its getJavaIdeSupport() method to provide the information necessary to generate IDE metadata files.

For synchronization, just execute jeka intellij: sync as usual.

docs.title: CLI Installation
docs.text: You don't need to install a JDK: JeKa downloads the version required by each project (about 200 MB, once). If a project does not specify any, JeKa uses the JDK set in JAVA_HOME, or downloads JDK 21.

docs.title: Windows
docs.text: iex "& { $(iwr -useb https://jeka.dev/install.ps1) } install check"

docs.title: SDKMAN!
docs.text:
sdk install jeka
To install applications with JeKa, also add ~/.jeka/apps to your PATH. Otherwise, they are installed in the directory of the current JeKa version.

docs.title: MacOS and Linux
docs.text:
curl -sL https://jeka.dev/install.sh | $(echo $0) -s - install check

$(echo $0) stands for your current shell. If the command fails (e.g. -zsh: command not found), replace it with bash: 

curl -sL https://jeka.dev/install.sh | bash -s - install check

The script installs JeKa in ~/.jeka/bin, and adds this directory to the PATH in your shell profile (e.g. ~/.zshrc). To install applications with JeKa, also add ~/.jeka/apps to your PATH.

Note

JeKa requires bash, curl, and unzip, usually available on macOS and Linux. On Ubuntu, install tools with: 

apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl unzip git gcc zlib1g-dev

docs.title: Manual installation
docs.text:
The manual installation is straightforward and may help when script installation fails.

  • Download latest JeKa distrib from maven central and download file named jeka-core-xxx-distrib.zip.
  • Unzip the content of the zip file and copy the content of the bin directory to [USER HOME]/.jeka/bin.
  • Add [USER HOME]/.jeka/bin and [USER HOME]/.jeka/apps to your PATH environment variable.
  • On macOS and Linux, make the scripts executable: chmod +x ~/.jeka/bin/jeka ~/.jeka/bin/jeka-update.
  • On Windows, edit the user PATH in System Properties > Environment Variables, then open a new terminal.

docs.title: Post Install
docs.text:
Installation via scripts may include a sanity check that triggers a JDK download (because of the check argument passed to the install script).

Once installed, you will rarely need to upgrade, as JeKa will execute the JeKa version specified in the application to run. However, you'll be able to upgrade your base install by executing: 

jeka-update

Open a new terminal session and execute the following command to access JeKa help: 

jeka --help

Next: Quick Start.

docs.title: Uninstall
docs.text: Delete ~/.jeka, which contains JeKa, its cache, installed applications and global.properties, then remove it from your PATH (in your shell profile, or in the Windows environment variables). With SDKMAN!, also execute sdk uninstall jeka <version>.

docs.title: Docker Image - Zero Install
docs.text:
JeKa can be executed using the Docker image jekadev/jeka.

To do this, execute:

  • Linux/macOS: docker run -v $HOME/.jeka/cache4c:/cache -v .:/workdir jekadev/jeka [JEKA ARGUMENTS]
  • Windows PowerShell: docker run -v ${HOME}\.jeka\cache4c:/cache -v ${PWD}:/workdir jekadev/jeka [JEKA ARGUMENTS]
  • Windows cmd: docker run -v %USERPROFILE%\.jeka\cache4c:/cache -v %cd%:/workdir jekadev/jeka [JEKA ARGUMENTS]

Note

-v $HOME/.jeka/cache4c:/cache

Tells JeKa to use a specific cache when running with a container, as JDK or other tools cached by JeKa may differ from the ones used by the host system.

-v .:/workdir

Lets JeKa operate in the current directory of the host machine.

[JEKA ARGUMENTS]

Stands for regular JeKa arguments you would pass to JeKa command line such as project: pack or --help.

docs.title: Migrating from JeKa 0.10
docs.text: This page helps you migrate from JeKa 0.10 to JeKa 0.11. To migrate from Maven, see Migrate a Maven Project.

docs.title: Command Line and Wrapper
docs.text:
The command line has been unified: jekaw has been replaced by jeka.

The wrapper is now entirely included in the shell scripts.

The jeka.version property is now located in the jeka.properties file along with other properties.

docs.title: Project Structure
docs.text:
The nested jeka directory has been removed in favor of a flat structure.

Also, the entire wrapper is contained inside shell scripts, so the jeka/wrapper directory is no longer needed.

  • jeka/def directory -> jeka-src
  • jeka/output -> jeka-output
  • jeka/.work -> .jeka-work
  • jeka/local.properties -> jeka.properties
  • jekaw.bat -> jeka.ps1
  • jekaw -> jeka
  • jeka/project-dependencies.txt -> jeka.project.deps
  • jeka/project-libs directory -> libs

docs.title: Major API Changes
docs.text:
• KBean classes are now suffixed with KBean instead of JkBean (e.g., ProjectKBean).
  • JkBean.getBean() -> KBean.load()

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• jeka.classpath.inject -> jeka.classpath
  • KBean field reference has changed from myKBean#xxx to @myKBean.xxx.

docs.title: Command Line
docs.text:
• KBean method invocation has changed from myKBean#pack to myKBean: pack.

Example: project#pack project#tests.skip=true

Is now: project: pack test.skip=true

  • Use jeka --help as a starting point for command-line help.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text: Welcome to JeKa! This guide will help you get up and running in minutes.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
You can get JeKa in two ways:

  • IntelliJ Plugin (Recommended): Install the JeKa Plugin. It's the fastest way to start, providing wizards for scripts, apps, and Spring Boot projects.
  • CLI: Install JeKa CLI manually or via SDKMAN!: sdk install jeka.

docs.title: Choose Your Path
docs.text:
This guide covers several use cases:

  • Create scripts in Java to automate your tasks.
  • Create a Base Application or Library for simple, pure Java projects.
  • Create a Java Project for more complex, standard layouts.
  • Create a Spring Boot Project with a pre-configured setup.

IntelliJ IDEA Users

After scaffolding or modifying dependencies, synchronize your project by executing: 

jeka intellij: sync

docs.title: Create Scripts
docs.text:
Create a directory to host the codebase. Navigate into it and execute: 

jeka base: scaffold
This generates a structure as: 
.                        <- Project root directory
├── jeka-src             <- Source dir for JeKa scripts and configuration code
│   └── Script.java     
├── jeka.properties      <- JeKa configuration (Java and JeKa version, default parameters...)
├── jeka.ps1             <- Optional PowerShell script to run JeKa on Windows
└── jeka                 <- Optional bash script to run JeKa on Linux/macOS
This script class looks like: jeka-src/Script.java
import dev.jeka.core.tool.JkDoc;
import dev.jeka.core.tool.KBean;

@JkDoc("Minimalist script for demo purpose.")
class Script extends KBean {

    @JkDoc("Person to whom the greeting is intended")
    public String name = "World";

    @JkDoc("Print greeting on console")
    public void hello() {
        String greetings = "Hello " + name + " !";
        System.out.println(greetings);
    }
}

docs.title: Run methods
docs.text:
You can run the method hello() and change the parameter, by executing: 

jeka hello name="JeKa"
The first execution may download the JDK set in jeka.properties (about 200 MB), if it is not already in the cache.

This displays the following text on the console: 

Hello JeKa !

docs.title: Write Extra Methods
docs.text:
You can add extra methods relying or not on third-party dependencies as: 

import com.github.lalyos.jfiglet.FigletFont;
import com.google.common.base.Strings;
import dev.jeka.core.tool.JkDep;
import dev.jeka.core.tool.KBean;

@JkDep("com.github.lalyos:jfiglet:0.0.9")
@JkDep("com.google.guava:guava:33.3.1-jre")
class Script extends KBean {

    public void header() throws Exception {
        System.out.println(Strings.repeat("-", 80));
        System.out.println(FigletFont.convertOneLine("Hello Ascii Art !"));
        System.out.println(Strings.repeat("-", 80));
    }
}
Execute: 
jeka header
This will display the following text on the console: 
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  _   _      _ _            _             _ _      _         _     _ 
 | | | | ___| | | ___      / \   ___  ___(_|_)    / \   _ __| |_  | |
 | |_| |/ _ \ | |/ _ \    / _ \ / __|/ __| | |   / _ \ | '__| __| | |
 |  _  |  __/ | | (_) |  / ___ \\__ \ (__| | |  / ___ \| |  | |_  |_|
 |_| |_|\___|_|_|\___/  /_/   \_\___/\___|_|_| /_/   \_\_|   \__| (_)


--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Note

  • You can define multiple script methods in Script.java. These methods must be public, non-static, take no arguments, and return void.
  • You can rename Script.java to any name and place it in any package.
  • You can create multiple script classes. To run a specific script, use the class name, e.g., jeka script2: hi.
  • You can also use classes provided by JeKa without explicitly declaring them.

docs.title: KBeans
docs.text:
Every script should inherit from the KBean class.

KBeans can either be provided as source code (located in the jeka-src directory) or as compiled classes available in the classpath.

JeKa includes several standard KBeans, which you can list by running: 

jeka --doc

docs.title: Change Java Version
docs.text:
To change version of Java, edit jeka.properties: 

jeka.java.version=23
This will automatically download Java 23 (if not already installed) on the next method run.

docs.title: Source-Runnable Applications
docs.text:
Run hello from another directory: 

jeka -r /path/to/script/root-dir hello

Run a KBean method from a remote Git repository: 

jeka -r https://github.com/jeka-dev/demo-base-application base: info

JeKa acts as an application source manager, allowing you to run or install applications directly from their source code. For more details, see the Source-Runnable Applications tutorial.

docs.title: Create a Base Application or Library
docs.text:
JeKa's base mode is the simplest way to build pure Java applications or libraries. It avoids the complexity of traditional Maven/Gradle structures while supporting full-featured builds, testing, native compilation, and Docker packaging.

To create a new code structure, run the following command: 

jeka base: scaffold scaffold.kind=APP
This creates a structure like this: 
. 
├── jeka-src             <- Source root directory
│   ├── _dev             <- Optional package containing all non-prod (build and test)
│   │   ├── test
│   │   └── Custom.java  
│   └── app              <- Suggested base package for production code/resources
│       └── App.java     
├── jeka.properties      <- Build configuration (Java and JeKa version, KBean configurations, ...)
├── jeka.ps1             <- Optional PowerShell script to run JeKa on Windows
├── jeka                 <- Optional bash script to run JeKa on Linux/macOS
└── README.md            <- Describes available build commands

Follow the tutorial for more details.

docs.title: Create a Java Project
docs.text:
For more complex needs, Project mode provides a standard layout similar to Maven or Gradle, supporting multi-module builds and advanced dependency management.

To create a new project structure, execute: 

jeka project: scaffold
This generates a project structure as: 
.
├── src                  
│   ├── main
│   │   └── java         <- Java code
│   └── test
│       └── java         <- Java code for tests
├── jeka-src             <- Optional Java (or Kotlin) code for building the project
│   └── Custom.java      
├── jeka.project.deps    <- Dependency lists for compile, runtime and testing
├── jeka.properties      <- Build configuration (Java and JeKa version, KBean configurations, ...)
├── jeka.ps1             <- Optional PowerShell script to boot JeKa on Windows
├── jeka                 <- Optional bash script to boot JeKa on Linux/MacOS
└── README.md            <- Describes available build commands for building the project

Generated artifacts (JARs, reports) are stored in jeka-output, created on the first build.

Follow the tutorial for more details.

docs.title: Create a Spring Boot Project
docs.text:
To create a new Spring Boot project, execute: 

jeka -cp=dev.jeka:springboot-plugin project: scaffold springboot:

Without version, JeKa uses the plugin version matching its own version.

This generates the following project structure: 

.
├── src                  
│   ├── main             
│   │   ├── java
│   │   │   └── app
│   │   │       ├── Application.java      <- Spring Boot app class
│   │   │       └── Controller.java       <- REST controller
│   │   └── resources
│   │       └── application.properties
│   └── test             
│       └── java
│           └── app
│               └── ControllerIT.java     <- Integration Test for REST controller 
├── jeka-src             
│   └── Custom.java      <- Optional build class (if needed)
├── jeka.project.deps    <- Spring Boot and extra dependencies
├── jeka.properties      <- Build configuration 
├── jeka.ps1             
├── jeka                 
└── README.md            <- Describes available build commands for building the project
This contains a minimal workable project with production and test code.

docs.title: Modify Layout
docs.text:
You can choose a simpler code layout structure when scaffolding: 

jeka -cp=dev.jeka:springboot-plugin project: scaffold layout.style=SIMPLE layout.mixSourcesAndResources=true springboot:
You'll end up with the following code layout: 
.
├── src       <- Contains both Java code and resources    
├── test      <- Contains both Java code and resources for testing
To convert an existing project, see Simple Layout.

docs.title: Modify Dependencies
docs.text:
The dependencies are generated with the latest Spring Boot version: jeka.project.deps

[version]
org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-dependencies:4.2.0@pom

[compile]
org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-webmvc

[test]
org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-webmvc-test
You can start from here for modifying, adding code, tests and dependencies.

docs.title: Execute Commands
docs.text:
These are the most useful commands for developing Spring Boot applications.

Common Commands
jeka project: test       # Compiles and run tests
jeka project: pack       # Compiles and creates Bootable Jar
jeka project: runJar     # Runs the bootable JAR
jeka project: build      # All-in-one: compile, test, pack, and verification
jeka project: depTree    # Displays the dependency tree

jeka docker: build       # Creates Docker image containing the Spring Boot application
jeka docker: buildNative # Creates Docker image for the native-compiled application

docs.title: Customize Docker File
docs.text:
To reduce a Docker native image size, use a distroless base image. The native executable must be statically linked as libc is unavailable in such distributions. Configure it as follows: jeka.properties

@native.staticLink=MUSL
@docker.nativeBaseImage=gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12:nonroot

docs.title: Under the Hood
docs.text: JeKa consists of a single zero-dependency JAR file, along with two shell scripts (one PowerShell script for Windows and one Bash script for Linux/macOS).

docs.title: Inside the JeKa JAR
docs.text:
The JeKa JAR is structured as follows:

  • dev.jeka.core.tool package:

    Contains classes for running Java externally, including the dev.jeka.core.tool.Main class and the component model.

  • dev.jeka.core.tool.builtins package:

    Contains KBeans bundled with JeKa, such as ProjectKBean, DockerKBean or NativeKBean.

  • dev.jeka.core.api package:

Includes libraries for building projects. These classes can be easily used outside JeKa and embedded in your product. 

graph TD
    subgraph dev.jeka.core
        subgraph tool 
            engine[dev.jeka.core.tool]
            builtin[dev.jeka.core.tool.builtins]
        end

            file[dev.jeka.core.api.file]
            utils[dev.jeka.core.api.utils]
            misc[...]
        end


    end

    engine --> system

docs.title: Title
docs.text: Command line KBean notation

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
We need to differentiate KBean, methods, and properties when parsing command lines.

KBean names can be all lowercase, causing confusion with method names. Using @KBeanName method1 method2 ... might face conflict with @file-arguments and may require using shift key on some keyboards.

However, a colon as KBeanName: method1 method2 ... doesn't require to use shift key, despite being less noticeable.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Jeka adopts the colon notation for KBean.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: To mention default KBean, we'll simply use : as in jeka project: pack : e2e

docs.title: Title
docs.text: Property Name for Skipping Tests

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text: A unique property is required for skipping tests in both projects and bases. This ensures the same property can be applied when running commands like jeka base:pack or jeka project:pack. It also simplifies invoking builds directly from OS scripts.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: The property will be named jeka.test.skip, aligning with the $Maven$ equivalent maven.skip.test.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: To build without running tests, use the following commands: - jeka project:pack -Djeka.test.skip - jeka base:pack -Djeka.test.skip

docs.title: Title
docs.text: Default include patterns for running tests.

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text: By default, Maven runs only test classes suffixed with Test. In the opposite, IDEs and Gradle runs all tests.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Jeka will runs all the tests by default as it is consistent with IDE and not an isolated behavior in the java build tool landscape.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: When running jeka project: test, all tests are executed unless explicitly specified.

docs.title: Title
docs.text: Run All Tests When the Include Pattern Is Empty

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Accepted

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Test selection allows filtering tests based on class names or tag presence. How should we interpret the behavior when no include pattern is specified? Should it mean "include all" or "exclude all"?

At first glance, "exclude all" might seem more logical. However, the JUnit platform considers an empty include pattern to mean "include all."

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: We decided to follow the JUnit platform behavior, both for class names and tags.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text: Include all tests when the include pattern is empty.

docs.title: Dependency Management API
docs.text:
In JeKa, a dependency is something that can be resolved to a set of files by a JkDependencyResolver. Generally, a dependency resolves to one file (or folder), but it can also be none or many.

The classes are located in the dev.jeka.core.api.depmanagement package.

Tip

To declare the dependencies of a project, you generally only need a jeka.project.deps file. See Project API.

docs.title: Types of Dependency
docs.text:
A dependency is always an instance of JkDependency. There are three main types:

  • Coordinates (JkCoordinateDependency): modules hosted in a Maven or Ivy repository, resolved transitively as in Maven or Gradle.
  • Files (JkFileSystemDependency): files located on the file system, expected to be present when the build runs.
  • Computed files (JkComputedDependency): files produced by a computation, run only if the files are missing. A dependency on another project (JkLocalProjectDependency) is a specialization of this type.
graph TD

    JkCoordinateDependency --> JkTransitivityDependency
    JkTransitivityDependency --> JkDependency
    JkFileDependency --> JkDependency

    JkComputedDependency --> JkFileDependency
    JkFileSystemDependency --> JkFileDependency
    JkLocalProjectDependency --> JkComputedDependency
    JkLocalProjectDependency --> JkTransitivityDependency

JeKa uses Ivy 2.5.3 under the hood. Ivy is downloaded on first use and runs in a dedicated classloader, hidden from your code.

docs.title: String Notation
docs.text:
Coordinates are expressed as strings, in one of the following formats:

  • group:name
  • group:name:version
  • group:name:classifiers:version
  • group:name:classifiers:extension:version
  • group:name:classifiers::
  • group:name:classifiers:extension:
  • group:name:version@pom

classifiers can be a comma-separated list. The two formats ending with : specify classifiers or an extension without specifying the version.

Examples: 

org.slf4j:slf4j-api                              <-- The version is provided elsewhere (BOM, version provider)
org.slf4j:slf4j-api:2.0.16                       <-- Declares an exact version
org.mock-server:mockserver-netty:shaded:5.15.0   <-- Declares a dependency on the 'shaded' classifier
org.lwjgl:lwjgl:natives-linux:3.3.6              <-- Declares a dependency on the 'natives-linux' classifier
org.lwjgl:lwjgl:natives-linux::                  <-- Same, without specifying the version
org.slf4j:slf4j-bom:2.0.16@pom                   <-- Declares a BOM
org.slf4j:slf4j-bom::pom:2.0.16                  <-- Declares a BOM (equivalent notation)

Versions can also be dynamic, using the Ivy version matchers.

In Java, a coordinate dependency can be created from this notation:

JkCoordinateDependency dep = JkCoordinateDependency.of("com.google.guava:guava:33.4.8-jre")
        .withTransitivity(JkTransitivity.RUNTIME)
        .andExclusions("com.google.code.findbugs:jsr305");

docs.title: BOM
docs.text: To import a Maven BOM, reference its pom: org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-dependencies:3.3.6@pom. The versions it declares are then used for modules declared without version.

docs.title: File Dependencies
docs.text:
Mention the path of one or several files. If one of the files does not exist at resolution time, the build fails.

JkDependencySet deps = JkDependencySet.of()
        .andFiles("libs/my.jar", "libs/my.testingtool.jar");

docs.title: Computed Dependencies
docs.text:
If the specified files are not present, the computation runs to generate them. If some files are still missing afterwards, the build fails.

This is useful for depending on files produced by other projects or other build tools (Maven, Gradle, npm, ...). The computation is either a java.lang.Runnable or a JkProcess.

The following snippet creates a dependency set on two external projects, one built with Maven, the other with JeKa:

Path mavenProjectDir = Paths.get("../a-maven-project");
Path mavenProjectJar = mavenProjectDir.resolve("target/maven-project.jar");
JkProcess mavenBuild = JkProcess.of("mvn", "clean", "package")
        .setWorkingDir(mavenProjectDir);

JkProject jekaProject = JkProject.of()
        .setBaseDir(Paths.get("../a-jeka-project"));

JkDependencySet deps = JkDependencySet.of()
        .and(JkComputedDependency.of(mavenBuild, mavenProjectJar))
        .and(jekaProject.toDependency());

docs.title: Dependency Set
docs.text:
A JkDependencySet is an ordered set of dependencies used for a given purpose (compilation, testing, ...). It can contain any kind of JkDependency, and also defines:

  • A version provider, giving the version of the modules declared without version.
  • A set of transitive dependency exclusions, applied to all dependencies of the set.

It is immutable: each method returns a new set.

JkVersionProvider versionProvider = JkVersionProvider.of()
        .andBom("org.slf4j:slf4j-bom:2.0.16")
        .and("com.google.guava:guava", "33.4.8-jre");

JkDependencySet deps = JkDependencySet.of()
        .and("com.google.guava:guava")
        .and("org.slf4j:slf4j-simple")
        .and("org.apache.httpcomponents:httpclient:4.5.14")
        .andFiles("../libs/myjar.jar")
        .andGlobalExclusion("commons-logging:commons-logging")
        .withVersionProvider(versionProvider);

See the source code for all available operations.

docs.title: Transitivity
docs.text:
Maven scopes and Gradle configurations answer three questions at once: which part of the build needs the dependency, which transitive dependencies are fetched, and how the dependency is published. JeKa answers them separately:

  1. Each part of the build (compile, runtime, test) has its own dependency set, which can be derived from another.
  2. Each dependency can have its own transitivity.
  3. The published dependencies can be redefined at publication time.

JkTransitivity defines three levels:

  • NONE: Not transitive.
  • COMPILE: Also fetches transitive dependencies declared with the 'compile' scope in the published POM.
  • RUNTIME: Also fetches transitive dependencies declared with the 'compile' or 'runtime' scope in the published POM.

When no transitivity is specified, JeKa uses the most relevant one according to the context where the dependency is declared. Transitivity applies only to JkCoordinateDependency and JkLocalProjectDependency.

The following example configures the dependencies of a project. Runtime dependencies are derived from compile ones:

JkProject project = JkProject.of();
project.flatFacade.dependencies.compile
        .add("com.google.guava:guava:33.4.8-jre", JkTransitivity.NONE)
        .add("javax.servlet:javax.servlet-api:4.0.1");
project.flatFacade.dependencies.runtime
        .add("org.postgresql:postgresql:42.7.4")
        .modify(deps -> deps.withTransitivity("com.google.guava:guava", JkTransitivity.RUNTIME))
        .remove("javax.servlet:javax.servlet-api");
project.flatFacade.dependencies.test
        .add(JkDependencySet.Hint.first(), "org.mockito:mockito-core:5.22.0");

Hint controls the position of the dependency in the set, and thus its position in the classpath.

docs.title: Resolve Dependencies
docs.text:
JkDependencyResolver resolves a JkDependencySet to a JkResolveResult.

JkDependencySet deps = JkDependencySet.of()
        .and("org.apache.httpcomponents:httpclient:4.5.14");

JkDependencyResolver resolver = JkDependencyResolver.of(JkRepo.ofMavenCentral());
JkResolveResult result = resolver.resolve(deps);

// Navigate in the resolved dependency tree
System.out.println(result.getDependencyTree().toStringTree());
JkVersion version = result.getVersionOf(JkModuleId.of("commons-codec:commons-codec"));

// Get the resolved files, as a classpath
JkPathSequence files = result.getFiles();
files.forEach(System.out::println);

If you only need the files, JkDependencyResolver#resolveFiles returns them directly.

docs.title: Publication
docs.text:
JeKa can publish to both Maven and Ivy repositories, including Sonatype Nexus. As Maven and Ivy have different publication models, there is a specific API for each one.

Tip

To publish a project on a Maven repository without writing code, use the Maven KBean.

docs.title: Publish to a Maven Repository
docs.text:
JkMavenPublication publication = JkMavenPublication.of(project.asBuildable())
        .setModuleId("org.example:my-lib")
        .setVersion("1.0.0")
        .setRepos(JkRepoSet.of("https://my.org/repository/internal"))
        .customizeDependencies(deps -> deps   // adjust the published transitive dependencies
                .withTransitivity("com.google.guava:guava", JkTransitivity.RUNTIME));

publication.pomMetadata
        .setProjectName("My library")
        .setProjectUrl("https://my.project.url")
        .addLicense("Apache License V2.0", "https://www.apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0.html");

publication.publish();

The POM file is generated by JeKa. It contains the dependencies of the runtime classpath: with scope compile if they are also needed to compile the project, with scope runtime otherwise. Compile-only dependencies are not published.

The main, sources and javadoc JARs are published by default. With this API, you can also:

  • Publish additional artifacts, using putArtifact.
  • Produce and publish checksum files.
  • Publish unique snapshots (see JkRepo.publishConfig).
  • Provide metadata required by Maven Central.
  • Sign published artifacts with PGP. There is no need to install PGP, as JeKa embeds Bouncy Castle.
  • Publish to multiple repositories.

See a complete example here.

docs.title: Publish to an Ivy Repository
docs.text:
Publishing to an Ivy repository is similar:

JkProjectPublications.ivyPublication(project)
        .setRepos(JkRepoSet.of("https://my.org/ivy-repository"))
        .publish();

docs.title: Common Classes
docs.text:
• JkRepo and JkRepoSet represent download and publish repositories.
  • JkRepoProperties provides the repositories configured by properties.
  • JkDependencySet represents a set of dependencies.
  • JkDependencyResolver resolves dependencies to files and dependency trees.
  • JkCoordinateFileProxy gets a file from its coordinate, downloading it if needed.

docs.title: Docker API
docs.text: The Docker API provides classes for defining and building Docker images programmatically. It relies on the Docker CLI, so a Docker installation (e.g., Docker Desktop) is required to invoke Docker commands from Java code.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Define Dockerfiles and build-context directories programmatically.
  • Generate optimized Docker images (JVM-based and native) directly from a project definition (e.g., a JkProject instance).

docs.title: Classes
docs.text: The classes are located in package dev.jeka.core.api.tooling.docker.

docs.title: JkDocker
docs.text:
Provides helper methods to:

  • Execute Docker commands conveniently.
  • Retrieve a list of image names present locally.
JkDocker.of().execCmdLine("run --rm -p8080:8080 io.my-registry/my-image:latest");

docs.title: JkDockerBuild
docs.text:
Represents a Docker build context. It enables defining the build context directory and Dockerfile, as well as invoking Docker to build an image.

Key features include:

  • Define Dockerfiles and build-context directory contents programmatically.
  • Build images based on the defined build context.
  • Simplify Dockerfile editing:
  • Add a non-root user.
  • Copy files into the build context.
  • Adjust cursor position to insert build steps at specific locations.
  • And more...
Example
JkDockerBuild dockerBuild = JkDockerBuild.of()
    .setBaseImage("eclipse-temurin:21-jdk-alpine")
    .setExposedPorts(8080);

dockerBuild.dockerfileTemplate
    .addCopy(Paths.get("/users/me/jars/my-app.jar"), "/app/my-app.jar")
    .add("WORKDIR /app")
    .addEntrypoint("java", "-jar", "/app/my-app.jar");

dockerBuild.buildImageInTemp("my-image:latest");  // Create the Docker image in a random temp dir
Generated Dockerfile
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jdk-alpine
RUN addgroup --gid 1002 nonrootgroup && \
    adduser --uid 1001 -g 1002 --disabled-password nonroot
USER nonroot
COPY imported-files/my-app.jar /app/my-app.jar
WORKDIR /app
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "/app/my-app.jar"]
EXPOSE 8080

Key Notes:

  • The non-root user has been automatically added as part of the Dockerfile.
  • Jar files from the filesystem have been imported into the [build context]/imported-files directory.

For more details, refer to the Javadoc.

docs.title: JkDockerJvmBuild
docs.text:
An extension of JkDockerBuild that provides additional methods to:

  • Generate optimized JVM-based Docker images directly from a project definition.
  • Add agents to the program for runtime enhancements.
Example
JkDockerJvmBuild dockerBuild = JkDockerJvmBuild.of(project.asBuildable())
    .addAgent("io.opentelemetry.javaagent:opentelemetry-javaagent:2.10.0", "myAgentOption");

dockerBuild.buildImageInTemp("my-jvm-image:latest");  // Create the Docker image in a random temp dir

Generated Dockerfile

FROM eclipse-temurin:25-jre-alpine
RUN addgroup --gid 1002 nonrootgroup && \
    adduser --uid 1001 -g 1002 --disabled-password nonroot
RUN mkdir -p /app && chown -R nonroot:nonrootgroup /app \
    && mkdir -p /workdir && chown -R nonroot:nonrootgroup /workdir
USER nonroot
COPY agents /app/agents
COPY libs /app/libs
COPY snapshot-libs /app/snapshot-libs
COPY classpath.txt /app/classpath.txt
COPY resources /app/classes
COPY classes /app/classes
WORKDIR /workdir
ENTRYPOINT [ "java", "-javaagent:/app/agents/opentelemetry-javaagent-2.10.0.jar=myAgentOption", "-cp", "@/app/classpath.txt", "app.Main" ]
CMD []
Key Notes:

  • The Docker image is layered for optimal caching. If a class changes without modifying dependencies, only the final step is re-executed, significantly speeding up the image creation process.
  • The OpenTelemetry agent has been included and referenced in the command-line arguments.

docs.title: JkDockerNativeBuild
docs.text:
An extension of JkDockerBuild offering additional methods for creating compact and efficient native executable images.

Example: Creating a Minimalist Distroless Image

This approach produces images with a minimal package set to reduce the attack surface. It requires building a native executable with static linking on libc (e.g., using MUSL).

Example
JkNativeCompilation nativeCompilation = nativeKBean.createNativeCompilation(project.asBuildable())
    .setStaticLinkage(JkNativeCompilation.StaticLink.MUSL);

JkDockerNativeBuild dockerBuild = JkDockerNativeBuild.of(nativeCompilation);
dockerBuild.setBaseImage("gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12:nonroot");

dockerBuild.buildImageInTemp("my-jvm-image:latest");  // Create the Docker image in a random temp dir
Generated Dockerfile
FROM ghcr.io/graalvm/native-image-community:25.0.2-muslib AS build
COPY imported-files/j2objc-annotations-3.0.0.jar /root/cp/j2objc-annotations-3.0.0.jar
COPY imported-files/error_prone_annotations-2.28.0.jar /root/cp/error_prone_annotations-2.28.0.jar
COPY imported-files/checker-qual-3.43.0.jar /root/cp/checker-qual-3.43.0.jar
COPY imported-files/jsr305-3.0.2.jar /root/cp/jsr305-3.0.2.jar
COPY imported-files/listenablefuture-9999.0-empty-to-avoid-conflict-with-guava.jar /root/cp/listenablefuture-9999.0-empty-to-avoid-conflict-with-guava.jar
COPY imported-files/failureaccess-1.0.2.jar /root/cp/failureaccess-1.0.2.jar
COPY imported-files/guava-33.3.1-jre.jar /root/cp/guava-33.3.1-jre.jar
COPY imported-files/hello-jeka.jar /root/cp/hello-jeka.jar
COPY imported-files/jeka-native-image-arg-file-5771078964740361323.txt /argfile
RUN native-image @/argfile

FROM gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12:nonroot

COPY  --from=build /my-app /app/myapp

WORKDIR /app
ENTRYPOINT ["/app/myapp"]

Key Notes:

  • The native executable is generated within a container using a multi-stage build.
  • No non-root user has been created because the base image is inferred to already include one (based on its name).
  • Native-based Docker images can be created directly from Windows or macOS workstations without any prerequisites other than Docker.

docs.title: Files API
docs.text:
File manipulation is a key aspect of software development. Jeka extends the java.nio.file API by introducing additional concepts to offer a powerful and fluent API for performing common tasks with minimal effort.

The file-api classes are located in the dev.jeka.core.api.file package. Visit the Javadoc.

docs.title: JkPathFile
docs.text:
A simple wrapper for files (not folders). It provides copying, interpolation, checksum, deletion and creation methods.

Example
JkPathFile.of("my-new-file.txt")
    .fetchContentFrom("https://www.bgreco.net/fortune.txt")
    .copyToDir(Paths.get("my-folder"));

docs.title: JkPathTree
docs.text:
An Immutable root folder along a PathMatcher providing operations to copy, navigate, zip, iterate, or watch. This is a central class in Jeka API.

Examples
// copies all non java source files to another directory preserving structure
JkPathTree.of("src").andMatching(false, "**/*.java").copyTo(Paths.get("build/classes"));

// One liner to zip an entire directory
JkPathTree.of("build/classes").zipTo(Paths.get("mylib.jar"));

// Traverse the tree breadth first (as opposed to depth first) 
JkPathTree.of("build/classes").streamBreathFirst().forEach(file -> System.out.println(file));

// Compute MD5
String md5 = JkPathTree.of("src/main/java").checksum("MD5");

docs.title: JkPathSequence
docs.text:
An Immutable sequence of java.nio.file.Path providing methods for filtering or appending. Example

URL[] urls = JkPathSequence.of(paths)
                .and(embeddedLibs)
                .toUrls();

docs.title: JkPathMatcher
docs.text: An immutable java.nio.file.PathMatcher based on java.nio.file glob pattern or regexp. Used by JkPathTree to filter in/out files according name patterns.

docs.title: JkZipTree
docs.text: Same as JkPathTree but using a zip file instead of a directory. It allows you to manipulate a zip file as a regular folder.

docs.title: JkPathTreeSet
docs.text: An Immutable set of JkPathTree. Helpful to define a set of sources/resources and create jar/zip files.

docs.title: JkResourceProcessor
docs.text: A mutable processor for copying a set of files, preserving the structure and replacing some texts with others. Typically used for replacing tokens ${server.ip} with an actual values.

docs.title: Git API
docs.text: The Git API provides classes for conveniently working with Git in Java. The classes are part of the dev.jeka.core.api.tooling.git package.

docs.title: JkGit class
docs.text:
The JkGit class extends JkAbstractProcess, as JkProcess does, which means it inherits methods that make process execution easier.

Sequence of Git calls
JkGit git = JkGit.of(rootDir);
git
    .execCmdLine("add .")
    .execCmdLine("config user.name  jeka-bot")
    .execCmdLine("config user.email jeka-bot@github-action.com")
    .execCmdLine("commit -m update-javadoc --allow-empty")
    .execCmdLine("push");

The tool offers many useful methods for executing standard DevOps commands like checking the workspace state, retrieving commit messages, and viewing current tags. For more details, visit the Javadoc.

Convenient method calls
List<String> tagNames = git.getTagsOnCurrentCommit();
String commit         = git.getCurrentCommit();
String messageToken   = git.extractSuffixFromLastCommitMessage("release:");

docs.title: JkVersionFromGit class
docs.text:
This class infers project versions from Git information based on the current tag or branch.

  • If the current commit is on a tag and the workspace is clean, the returned version is the tag name, without the prefix.
  • Otherwise, the returned version is branch-name-SNAPSHOT (/ replaced by -), or short-commit-hash-SNAPSHOT if there is no current branch (detached HEAD).
JkVersionFromGit versionFromGit = JkVersionFromGit.of("v");  // consider only tags starting with 'v'
System.out.println(versionFromGit.getVersion());

versionFromGit.handleVersioning(project);

docs.title: Build Library
docs.text:
JeKa comes with a set of classes designed to help you programmatically accomplish build tasks. These classes are used to implement JeKa's engine and its bundled KBeans. You may find these classes useful for your own needs, as they cover the following concerns:

  • File manipulation.
  • Java specific actions (compilation, classloading, jar creation, ...). Visit Javadoc.
  • Kotlin specific actions (compilation, modules). Visit source code.
  • Cryptography signing. Visit source code.
  • Dependency management.
  • Project Building
  • Testing (run tests on junit-jupiter engine). Visit Javadoc.
  • Running external commands. Visit Javadoc.

docs.title: Native API
docs.text:
The Native API offers a JkNativeCompilation class that creates an executable file from compiled classes or JARs.

An easy way to get an instance is to call NativeKBean#createNativeCompilation, passing the project as a JkBuildable. This prepares everything for native compilation, applying the settings of the Native KBean. You can also start from a classpath, using JkNativeCompilation.ofClasspath. The class automatically downloads GraalVM, which includes the native-image executable used for compiling to native - you don't need to care about GraalVM installation.

It also provides helpful methods to add resources to the native executable.

Example

nativeKBean.createNativeCompilation(project.asBuildable())
    .setIncludesAllResources(true)
    .make(Paths.get("jeka-output/my-app"));
This code performs the following actions:

  • Checks if JeKa is running on GraalVM. If not, it fetches GraalVM 25 (if not already available).
  • Includes all project resources located in src/main/resources.
  • Fetches the metadata repository and adds it to the compilation classpath.
  • Uses the native-image GraalVM tool to compile the application into a native binary.

By default, JeKa will fetch GraalVM using the Foojay API unless the JEKA_GRAALVM_HOME environment variable is set. If the environment variable's value starts with DOWNLOAD_ (e.g., DOWNLOAD_21), the specified GraalVM version will be downloaded from the internet.

docs.title: Project API
docs.text: The JeKa Project API provides a high-level interface for building Java/JVM projects. JkProject is its entry point.

docs.title: Classes
docs.text: The classes are located in the dev.jeka.core.api.project package.

docs.title: JkProject
docs.text:
JkProject contains all the definitions for building a JVM project: source locations, dependencies, compilation, testing, packaging, and more. It offers extension points to integrate specific build behaviors.

The main members are:

project
├─ baseDir, outputDir, jvmTargetVersion, sourceEncoding, moduleId, version, duplicateConflictStrategy (getters and setters)
├─ artifactLocator (defines where artifact files are created)
├─ compilerToolChain
├─ dependencyResolver
├─ compilation  (produces binary files from production sources)
│  ├─ layout (location of source and resource files)
│  ├─ dependencies   (compile dependencies)
│  ├─ procDependencies  (annotation-processor dependencies, passed as -processorpath)
│  ├─ resourceProcessor
│  ├─ preCompileActions (including resource processing)
│  ├─ compileActions (including Java compilation. Compilation for other languages can be added here)
│  ├─ postCompileActions
│  └─ methods : addSourceGenerator(), addJavaCompilerOptions(), generateSources(), resolveDependenciesAsFiles(), run()
├─ test
│  ├─ compilation (same as above, for test sources)
│  ├─ processor
│  │  ├─ preActions
│  │  ├─ postActions
│  │  ├─ engineBehavior (progress display, JUnit platform launcher configuration)
│  │  └─ methods : setForkingProcess()
│  ├─ selection (include/exclude patterns and tags)
│  ├─ postActions
│  └─ methods : setSkipped(), setBreakOnFailures(), run()
├─ pack (produces binary, fat, sources and javadoc JARs)
│  ├─ actions
│  ├─ runtimeDependencies
│  ├─ javadocProcessor
│  ├─ manifestCustomizer
│  └─ methods : createBinJar(), createFatJar(), createSourceJar(), createJavadocJar(), customizeFatJarContent(), 
│               resolveRuntimeDependencies(), run()
├─ qualityCheck
│  └─ methods : add(), run()
├─ e2eTest
│  └─ methods : add(), run()
├─ flatFacade
└─ methods : clean(), fullBuild(), toDependency(), asBuildable(), getInfo(), displayDependencyTree(), getDependenciesAsXml()
See a detailed example here.

Note

The testing and packaging fields, and the pack() method, are deprecated. Use test, pack and pack.run().

In a KBean, get the project from the ProjectKBean:

import dev.jeka.core.api.project.JkProject;
import dev.jeka.core.api.testing.JkTestSelection;
import dev.jeka.core.tool.JkPostInit;
import dev.jeka.core.tool.KBean;
import dev.jeka.core.tool.builtins.project.ProjectKBean;

class Custom extends KBean {

    @JkPostInit(required = true)
    private void postInit(ProjectKBean projectKBean) {
        JkProject project = projectKBean.project;
        project.compilation.addJavaCompilerOptions("-Xlint:unchecked");
        project.test.selection.addExcludePatterns(JkTestSelection.IT_PATTERN);
    }
}

docs.title: Flat Facade
docs.text:
JkProject offers a simplified facade to configure common settings without delving into its structure.

JkProjectFlatFacade projectFacade = JkProject.of().flatFacade;
projectFacade
       .setModuleId("dev.jeka:sample-javaplugin")
       .setVersionFromGitTag()
       .setMixResourcesAndSources()
       .setLayoutStyle(JkCompileLayout.Style.SIMPLE)
       .addTestExcludeSuffixIf(true, "IT");
projectFacade.dependencies.compile
       .add("com.google.guava:guava:33.4.8-jre")
       .add("org.projectlombok:lombok:1.18.36");
projectFacade.dependencies.runtime
       .remove("org.projectlombok:lombok")
       .add("com.github.djeang:vincer-dom:1.2.0");
projectFacade.dependencies.test
       .add("org.junit.jupiter:junit-jupiter:5.12.2");
projectFacade.doPack();  // compile and create jar

docs.title: Project Dependencies
docs.text:
JeKa uses three classpaths, each one derived from the previous ones:

  • Compile classpath: Needed to compile the classes.

  • Runtime classpath: Needed to run the application, or embedded in the JAR, or published as transitive dependencies. It is constructed from the compile classpath, where other libraries can be added or removed.

  • Test classpath: Needed to compile and run the tests. It is constructed by merging the compile and runtime classpaths, where other libraries can be added or removed.

There is also a processor path for annotation processors, independent of these classpaths.

Dependencies can be declared programmatically, as above, or in a jeka.project.deps file. See String Notation for the accepted formats.

docs.title: jeka.project.deps
docs.text:
Project dependencies can be declared in the [PROJECT_DIR]/jeka.project.deps text file.

Example: 

[version]
org.junit:junit-bom:5.12.1@pom    # use this BOM as a version provider for all JUnit dependencies
org.postgresql:postgresql:42.5.0
org.glassfish.jaxb:jaxb-*:4.0.5   # use a wildcard to specify the version of several modules

[compile]
com.google.guava:guava:33.4.8-jre
org.lwjgl:lwjgl:natives-linux:3.3.6  # specify the 'natives-linux' classifier for lwjgl
org.glassfish.jaxb:jaxb-runtime      # version for org.glassfish.jaxb:jaxb-* is specified above
../module-utils                      # specify a project directory located on the file system

[compile-only]
jakarta.servlet:jakarta.servlet-api:6.1.0
org.openjfx:javafx-base:${jeka.platform.os}:21.0.2  # properties are interpolated
com.github.tjake:jlama-native:${maven.classifier.os}-${maven.classifier.arch}:: # specify a classifier without specifying the version

[runtime]
org.postgresql:postgresql

[test]
org.junit.jupiter:junit-jupiter
org.junit.platform:junit-platform-launcher
org.fluentlenium:fluentlenium-junit:3.2.0
    !org.apache.httpcomponents:httpclient  # exclude httpclient from 'fluentlenium-junit' transitive dependencies
!!commons-logging:commons-logging          # exclude commons-logging from all dependencies of this section

[processor]
org.mapstruct:mapstruct-processor:1.6.3   # 'org.mapstruct:mapstruct' must also be in [compile]

A line starting with ! excludes a module from the transitive dependencies of the dependency declared just above. A line starting with !! excludes a module from the transitive dependencies of all the dependencies of the section.

[version] Specifies the versions of dependencies to use when not explicitly defined. You can include all versions defined in a BOM by referencing its coordinates and appending @pom. The section inherits definitions from the [version] section of the jeka.project.deps file located in the parent directory.

[compile] Specifies dependencies required for both compiling and running the project.

[compile-only] Specifies dependencies required only for compiling the project, which are excluded at runtime.

[runtime] Specifies dependencies required only for running the project.

[test] Specifies dependencies for the test classpath, in addition to those of the [compile], [compile-only] and [runtime] sections.

[processor] Specifies annotation-processor dependencies (e.g. Lombok, MapStruct). These are passed to the compiler via -processorpath and are not added to the compile or runtime classpaths. Declare the annotations used in your code in [compile] or [compile-only] as well. Generated sources are written to jeka-output/generated-sources/annotation-processors.

Tip

If you're using the JeKa plugin for IntelliJ, press ctrl+<space> for autocomplete suggestions.

Resolve Dependencies Programmatically

To resolve the dependencies of the runtime classpath:

JkResolveResult result = project.pack.resolveRuntimeDependencies();     // includes the dependency tree
List<Path> classpath = project.pack.resolveRuntimeDependenciesAsFiles();  // JAR files only

Display the Dependency Tree on the Console

Use JkProject.displayDependencyTree().

Change the Maven Repository

By default, dependencies are resolved using the Maven Central repository. You can change it using properties, or programmatically:

project.dependencyResolver.setRepos(JkRepoSet.of("https://my.company/repo"));

docs.title: Display Generic Info
docs.text: JkProject.getInfo() returns a text with project info such as locations, source file count, version, and module ID.

docs.title: Build Project
docs.text:
The phases of the build can be invoked using the following methods:

  • project.compilation.generateSources(): Generates sources if any source generators are registered.
  • project.compilation.run(): Runs the entire compilation process, including source generation and other registered compilation tasks.
  • project.test.run(): Compiles and runs tests. Production code is compiled first, if not done yet.
  • project.pack.run(): Creates the main JAR and any additional artifacts configured. Production code is compiled first, if not done yet. Tests are not run.
  • project.qualityCheck.run(): Runs the registered quality checkers.
  • project.e2eTest.run(): Runs the registered end-to-end tests.
  • project.fullBuild(): Runs clean, test, pack and end-to-end tests.

In the next sections, we detail some classes involved in the build process.

docs.title: JkProjectCompilation
docs.text:
Handles the compilation tasks for a JkProject, for both production and test code. It offers configuration methods for defining:

  • The locations of source files and compiled classes (layout).
  • Dependencies required for compilation (dependencies).
  • Annotation-processor dependencies passed as -processorpath (procDependencies).
  • The compilation options.
  • Source code generators attached to the compilation task.
  • Additional pre and post actions tied to the compilation phase.
  • Interpolators for resource processing (resourceProcessor).

docs.title: JkProjectSourceGenerator
docs.text:
Implement this interface to define a source generator.

class MyGenerator implements JkProjectSourceGenerator {

    @Override
    public String getDirName() {
        return "my-generator";  // directory name, under the generated sources dir
    }

    @Override
    public void generate(JkProject project, Path generatedSourceDir) {
        JkPathFile.of(generatedSourceDir.resolve("org/example/Info.java"))
                .createIfNotExist()
                .write("package org.example; public class Info {}");
    }
}

Register it using project.compilation.addSourceGenerator(new MyGenerator()). Sources are then generated during compilation, or when calling project.compilation.generateSources().

docs.title: App KBean
docs.text:
Provides a way to install, update, or remove applications from the user PATH.

Applications are installed from a Git repository and built by the client before installation.

Runtime modes: - JVM: Runs on a Jeka-managed JDK, installed in ~/.jeka/apps - NATIVE: Compiled as a native executable - BUNDLE: Runs with a tailored JRE bundled with the app, which JeKa opens for you to install. macOS and Windows only.

AppKBean manages the installation, update, and discovery of applications from remote repositories or catalogs.

For a practical guide on running and installing applications from source, see the Source-Runnable Applications tutorial.

Key Features

  • Installs applications from remote Git repositories.
  • Supports JVM, Native, and Bundle runtime modes.
  • Manages application updates and uninstallation.
  • Facilitates application discovery via catalogs.
  • Provides security through trusted source verification.

docs.title: Install Applications
docs.text:
jeka app: install repo=REPO_URL

JeKa may ask to trust the URL, to choose a version if the repository has tags, and to choose a name if neither name nor a catalog application is specified. These questions need a terminal: without it, the command fails. The version cannot be set with a #tag suffix.

To install without any question, as in a script or CI, trust the URL first, then pass the tag and the name:

jeka app: trustUrl url=github.com/my-org/
jeka app: install repo=https://github.com/my-org/my-app.git tag=1.2.0 name=my-app

Use tag=@ to install the last commit of the default branch.

Note

Add ~/.jeka/apps to your PATH before installing applications. Otherwise, they are installed in the JeKa distribution directory, and may be lost when switching versions (e.g. with SDKMAN!).

Applications can be installed in different runtime modes:

docs.title: Runtime Modes
docs.text:
• JVM (default): JVM application running on a JDK managed by Jeka. Binary is installed in ~/.jeka/apps and available in PATH.
  • NATIVE: Native executable compiled ahead-of-time using GraalVM.
  • BUNDLE: Application bundled with a tailored JRE. JeKa opens the folder holding the bundle (a .dmg on macOS), for you to install it. macOS and Windows only.

docs.title: Using the runtime parameter
docs.text:
Install in native mode: 

jeka app: install repo=REPO_URL runtime=NATIVE

Install as a bundle: 

jeka app: install repo=REPO_URL runtime=BUNDLE

Examples: Install kill8 app as a JVM application: 

jeka app: install repo=https://github.com/djeang/kill8 name=killport
or use the GitHub repo shorthand 
jeka app: install repo=kill8@djeang

or use an alternative application name or runtime mode 

jeka app: install repo=https://github.com/djeang/kill8 name=killport runtime=NATIVE

docs.title: List Installed Applications
docs.text:
jeka app: list
This displays the name of the applications, along with their repo, version/status, and runtime type. 
App Name   │ Repo                                      │ Version  │ Status     │ Runtime │ 
calculator │ https://github.com/djeang/Calculator-jeka │ latest   │ up-to-date │ jvm     │ 
kill8      │ https://github.com/djeang/kill8           │ <master> │ up-to-date │ native  │

docs.title: Update Applications
docs.text:
jeka app: update name=kill8
The update depends on what is currently installed:

  • A version tag (e.g. 1.2.0): JeKa looks for higher version tags and proposes to update to the highest one.
  • Any other tag (e.g. latest): the tag is kept, and its content is refreshed if it has changed.
  • No tag: the application is updated to the latest commit.

docs.title: Uninstall Applications
docs.text:
jeka app: uninstall name=kill8

If no app has this name, the command fails, as app: update does. Add force=true to only get a warning, as in a cleanup script.

docs.title: Catalogs
docs.text: Application catalogs are curated collections of Jeka applications that can be easily discovered and installed. Catalogs make it simple to share and distribute applications across teams or communities.

docs.title: Viewing Catalogs
docs.text:
Display all registered catalogs: 

jeka app: catalog

This shows the catalog names, descriptions, and URLs sorted by repository.

Display applications in a specific catalog: 

jeka app: catalog name=demo

This lists all applications available in the specified catalog, showing:

  • Application name and description
  • Application type (CLI, SERVER, SERVER-UI, etc.)
  • Commands to run or install the application
  • Available runtime modes (JVM, NATIVE, BUNDLE)

docs.title: Installing from Catalogs
docs.text:
Install an application using the catalog shorthand: 

jeka app: install repo=cowsay@demo

The format is appName@catalogName. This is equivalent to providing the full repository URL.

docs.title: Creating a Catalog
docs.text:
To add a catalog, add the following lines to your ~/.jeka/global.properties file: 

jeka.catalog.xxx.repo=[http location or git repo url]
jeka.catalog.xxx.desc=[Description of the catalog]
where xxx stands for the name of your catalog.

The jeka.catalog.xxx.repo value can be:

  1. A full URL to the catalog properties file
  2. A GitHub organization name (looks for jeka-catalog repository)
  3. A GitHub organization/repository path

Valid examples: 

# GitHub organization - expects jeka-catalog repo at root
jeka.catalog.djeang.repo=djeang
jeka.catalog.djeang.desc=Personal applications

# GitHub organization/repository - expects jeka-catalog.properties at root
jeka.catalog.demo.repo=jeka-dev/demo
jeka.catalog.demo.desc=Demo applications

# Direct URL to catalog file
jeka.catalog.custom.repo=https://raw.githubusercontent.com/myorg/my-catalog/refs/heads/main/jeka-catalog.properties
jeka.catalog.custom.desc=Custom application catalog

docs.title: Catalog File Format
docs.text:
A catalog file is a properties file named jeka-catalog.properties containing application definitions:

# Application entries follow the pattern: app.<name>.<property>=<value>

app.cowsay.repo=https://github.com/jeka-dev/demo-cowsay
app.cowsay.desc=Java port of the Cowsay famous CLI.
app.cowsay.type=CLI
app.cowsay.native=true
app.cowsay.bundle=false

app.demo-springboot-angular.repo=https://github.com/jeka-dev/demo-project-springboot-angular
app.demo-springboot-angular.desc=Manage a list of users. Written in Spring Boot and Angular.
app.demo-springboot-angular.type=SERVER-UI
app.demo-springboot-angular.native=false
app.demo-springboot-angular.bundle=true

Available application properties:

  • repo (required): Git repository URL of the application
  • desc (required): Short description of the application
  • type (optional): Application type (CLI, SERVER, SERVER-UI, LIBRARY, etc.)
  • native (optional): Set to true if the app supports native compilation (default: false)
  • bundle (optional): Set to true if the app supports bundled distribution (default: false)

docs.title: Built-in Catalogs
docs.text: JeKa comes with built-in catalogs (demo, djeang, thirdparty), listed by jeka app: catalog. Additional catalogs can be registered in ~/.jeka/global.properties. A project's jeka.properties is not read.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
Repositories from github.com/jeka-dev/ are trusted by default. See Trust and Security for the different ways to trust other URLs, and the behavior without a terminal.

Trusted URL prefixes are stored in the jeka.app.url.trusted property, located in the ~/.jeka/global.properties file. You can adjust this property later to make it more or less restrictive, or add a prefix by running jeka app: trustUrl url=github.com/djeang/. Prefixes are separated by spaces. The check compares whole path segments of the Git URL, after removing the protocol, user and tag: github.com/djeang trusts github.com/djeang/xxx, but not github.com/djeang-other/xxx. URLs containing .., //, %, \ or spaces are never trusted.

Prefer entries naming a single repository (github.com/djeang/kill8).

Example: jeka.app.url.trusted=github.com/djeang/ will trust URLs formed as:

  • https://github.com/djeang/xxx
  • https://my-user-name@github.com/djeang/xxx
  • git@github.com:djeang/xxx.git
  • ssh://git@github.com/djeang/xxx.git

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
This KBean exposes the following fields:

Field Description repo [String] Git Remote repository URL of the app to install. name [String] Specifies the name of the app to install, update or uninstall. tag [String] Git tag to install, or '@' for the last commit of the default branch. When set, no version is asked. force [boolean] If true, 'uninstall' does not fail when no app has the specified name. description [String] Short description of the app provided by the application author. url [String] Specifies the url to trust. runtime [enum:RuntimeMode] Runtime mode for app installation:- JVM (default): Runs on a Jeka-managed JDK, installed in ~/.jeka/apps (on your PATH)- NATIVE: Compiled as a native executable, installed in ~/.jeka/apps (on your PATH)- BUNDLE: Bundled with a tailored JRE. JeKa opens the folder holding the bundle (a .dmg on macOS), for you to install it. macOS and Windows only..

This KBean exposes the following methods:

Method Description catalog List application catalogs. install Builds and installs the app to make it available in PATH.Use repo=[Git URL] to set the source repository.Use runtime=JVM\|NATIVE\|BUNDLE to specify the runtime mode. list Lists installed Jeka commands in the user's PATH. trustUrl Adds permanently the url to the trusted list.The urls starting with the specified prefix will be automatically trusted.Use 'url=my.host/my.path/' to specify the prefix. uninstall Uninstalls an app from the user's PATH.Use name=[app-name] to specify the app. update Updates an app from the given name.Use name=[app-name] to specify the app name.

docs.title: Base KBean
docs.text:
Manages the build and execution of code located in 'jeka-src' directory.

The code can stand for either an application or a library. For applications, code should contain a class including a main method to:

  • Run application
  • Create bootable jar
  • Create bootable fat jar, and create Docker images

BaseKBean is similar to ProjectKBean, but it facilitates building JVM-based code hosted entirely in the jeka-src folder with a simpler classpath organization.

  • Single Classpath: By default, there is a single classpath. However, if a _dev package exists in the code structure, its contents are excluded when creating JARs, native executables, or Docker images. Typically, build and test classes are placed in _dev for application builds.
  • Dependency Declaration: Dependencies are declared by annotating any class with the @JkDep annotation. Dependencies within the _dev package are excluded from production artifacts.

Key Features

  • Resolves dependencies, compiles code, and runs tests.
  • Creates various types of JAR files out-of-the-box: regular, fat, shaded, source, and Javadoc JARs.
  • Infers project versions from Git metadata.
  • Executes packaged JARs.
  • Displays dependency trees and project setups.
  • Scaffolds skeletons for new projects.
  • Plugin Development: Particularly well-suited for developing reusable JeKa plugins (KBeans), as it allows you to write your plugin code directly in jeka-src and test it immediately.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
Create an application, a JeKa plugin, or a simple script: 

jeka base: scaffold scaffold.kind=APP
jeka base: scaffold scaffold.kind=PLUGIN
jeka base: scaffold

Build and run: 

jeka base: build              # run tests, then create the JAR
jeka base: pack               # create the JAR only
jeka base: runMain            # run the application from its classes
jeka base: runJar programArgs="arg1 arg2"
jeka base: info               # show the main class, classpath, manifest, ...

docs.title: Configuration
Dependencies
docs.text:
Declare dependencies by annotating classes. Those declared in the _dev package are for tests and build only:

jeka-src/_dev/Custom.java
package _dev;

import dev.jeka.core.tool.JkDep;
import dev.jeka.core.tool.JkPostInit;
import dev.jeka.core.tool.KBean;
import dev.jeka.core.tool.builtins.base.BaseKBean;

@JkDep("org.junit.jupiter:junit-jupiter")
@JkDep("org.junit:junit-bom:6.0.3@pom")
class Custom extends KBean {

    @JkPostInit(required = true)
    private void postInit(BaseKBean baseKBean) {
        baseKBean.setModuleId("org.example:my-app").setVersion("1.0.0");
        baseKBean.packActions.append("say-done", () -> System.out.println("Packed!"));
    }
}

The postInit method customizes the build. Add @custom=on to jeka.properties to have Custom always initialized.

Note

@JkDep values are read from the source code before compilation: write them as string literals, not constants.

Example

  • Base Application: The BaseKBean is set as the default KBean in jeka.properties. The accompanying README.md file details the available base: methods that can be invoked.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
This KBean exposes the following fields:

Field Description jvmOptions [String] Space separated list of options to pass to the JVM that will run the program. programArgs [String] Space separated list of program arguments to pass to the command line running the program. moduleId [String] Group and name for publication, formatted as 'groupId:nameId'. jarType [enum:JkProjectPackaging$JarType] Type of jar to produce for the main artifact. gitVersioning.enable [boolean] If true, the version is computed from the current Git branch/tag. gitVersioning.tagPrefix [String] Some prefer to prefix version tags like 'v1.3.1' instead of simply using '1.3.1'. In such cases, this value can be set to 'v' or any other chosen prefix. scaffold.kind [enum:JkBaseScaffold$Kind] Kind of Jeka base to generate. scaffold.jekaVersion [String] Set a specific jeka.version to include in jeka.properties. NO: no jeka.version specified, [EMPTY]: last version found in Maven Central. scaffold.jekaLocation [String] Set a specific jeka.distrib.location to include in jeka.properties. scaffold.jekaDistribRepo [String] Set a specific jeka.distrib.repo to include in jeka.properties. scaffold.extraJekaProps [String] Coma separated string representing properties to add to jeka.properties. If this file already exists, they are appended to it, except the ones already declared. scaffold.rawJekaPropsContentPath [Path] Set the path of a file containing the exact content of the jeka.properties file to generate.An existing jeka.properties file is kept as is.If this field is set, all others related to jeka.properties generation are ignored.

This KBean exposes the following methods:

Method Description build Runs tests then 'pack'. depTree Displays exported dependency tree on console. info Displays info about this base KBean. pack Creates runnable fat jar and optional artifacts. runJar Runs fat jar. runMain Launches application. scaffold Creates a skeleton in the current working directory. test Launches test suite.

docs.title: Bundle KBean
docs.text:
Bundle a self-contained Java app (containing JRE) using jpackage and jlink tools.

This plugin creates a self-contained app and allows configuring the jpackage and jlink tools.

This integrates with ProjectKBean for project-specific setups, handles file system operations to prepare input directories, and invokes jpackage and jlink tools.

docs.title: Creates a customized self-contained app
docs.text:
Thanks to jpackage and jlink tools, this KBean creates self-contained Java applications or installers tailored for the host system.

To create such a bundle, execute: jeka bundle: pack.

The application or installer will be created in [project dir]/jeka-output dir.

If you want to create this bundle along other artifacts while executing jeka project: pack, you need to specify the following property in jeka.properties: 

@bundle.projectPack=true

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• customJre - If true, creates a custom JRE containing only the Java modules used by the application, using jlink. This reduces bundle size.

  • projectPack - If true, the bundled application is created automatically when executing jeka project: pack.

  • includeRuntimeLibs - If true (default), runtime dependencies are included in the packaged application. Set to false when using fat JARs.

docs.title: JPackage Options
docs.text:
Configure jpackage using the @bundle.jpackage.options prefix in jeka.properties. Declare one property per option, named after the platform (all, windows, linux or mac) and the option:

# Common options for all platforms
@bundle.jpackage.options.all.--name=MyApp
@bundle.jpackage.options.all.--vendor="My Company"
@bundle.jpackage.options.all.--description="My Application"

# Windows-specific options
@bundle.jpackage.options.windows.--icon=media/icon.ico
@bundle.jpackage.options.windows.--type=msi

# Linux-specific options
@bundle.jpackage.options.linux.--icon=media/icon.png
@bundle.jpackage.options.linux.--type=deb

# macOS-specific options
@bundle.jpackage.options.mac.--icon=media/icon.icns
@bundle.jpackage.options.mac.--type=dmg

Suggested options:

  • --name - Application name
  • --vendor - Vendor name
  • --description - Application description
  • --icon - Application icon (platform-specific format)
  • --type - Package type (app-image, exe, msi, deb, rpm, pkg, dmg)
  • --add-modules - Additional JPMS modules to include (or use JDEPS-COMPUTE to auto-detect)
  • --java-options - JVM options for the application
  • --runtime-image - Path to custom JRE

docs.title: JLink Options
docs.text:
When using customJre=true, configure jlink using the @bundle.jlink.options prefix:

# Common jlink options
@bundle.jlink.options.all.--compress=2
@bundle.jlink.options.all.--bind-services=

# Platform-specific options
@bundle.jlink.options.windows.--strip-debug=

Suggested options:

  • --add-modules - Modules to include in custom JRE
  • --bind-services - Include service provider modules
  • --compress - Compression level (0=none, 1=constant strings, 2=ZIP)
  • --disable-plugin - Disable specific plugins
  • --limit-module - Limit universe of observable modules

docs.title: Automatic Module Detection
docs.text:
Use JDEPS-COMPUTE to automatically detect required JPMS modules:

@bundle.jpackage.options.all.--add-modules=JDEPS-COMPUTE
