JkMultiValue objects support nesting, allowing you to create hierarchical data structures with multiple levels of key-value pairs.

docs.title: JeKa Basics
docs.text: JeKa is not just a build tool; it's a powerful companion for Java development that allows you to run Java code as scripts with zero ceremony. This tutorial will walk you through the core concepts of JeKa by creating and running simple scripts.

docs.title: Create a basic script
docs.text:
To create a basic JeKa structure, execute: 

jeka base: scaffold

This generates a jeka-src/Script.java file, which is an example of Java code invokable from the command line.

import dev.jeka.core.tool.JkDoc;
import dev.jeka.core.tool.KBean;

class Script extends KBean {

    @JkDoc("Person to whom the greeting is intended")
    public String name = "World";

    @JkDoc("Print greeting on console")
    public void hello() {
        String greetings = "Hello " + name + " !";
        System.out.println(greetings);
    }

}

IntelliJ IDEA Users

The JeKa IntelliJ Plugin is the recommended way to work with JeKa. If you prefer using the CLI for synchronization, execute jeka intellij: sync to update IDE metadata. If IntelliJ does not reflect changes, you can re-initialize the project with jeka intellij: initProject.

By default, jeka-src is declared as a test source folder. You can isolate it in its own module by executing jeka intellij: sync splitModule=true.

Execute jeka hello. A Hello World message is printed on the console. 

Hello World !

Execute jeka hello name=JeKa. A Hello JeKa message is printed on the console. 

Hello JeKa !

Add a similar hi method in Script.java: 

public void hi() {
    System.out.println("Hi " + name + " !");
}
... and execute jeka hi. You will notice that your change has been automatically taken into account without any extra action on your part.

You can add as many public void no-args methods or public fields in your scripts. The accepted public field types are mentioned here.

Tip

You can document your script by annotating the class, public fields, or public methods with the @JkDoc annotation. This will be visible when executing: jeka script: --doc. Note that only the part before the first line break of the doc content will be displayed as a summary.

docs.title: Define JDK version
docs.text:
JeKa can automatically manage the JDK used to run your scripts. This ensures reproducibility across different machines.

Edit jeka.properties: 

jeka.java.version=23
Executing jeka hello will now trigger a download of JDK 23 (if not already present) before executing the script. JeKa caches downloaded JDKs in ~/.jeka/cache/jdks.

You can also specify a distribution: 

jeka.java.version=21
jeka.java.distrib=corretto

If you prefer to use a local JDK, specify its path: 

jeka.java.version=22
jeka.jdk.22=/my/jdks/22-corretto

Note

The JDK location can also be passed on the command line, as -Djeka.jdk.22=/my/jdks/22-corretto.

docs.title: Define JeKa version
docs.text:
To ensure your script always runs with a compatible JeKa version, regardless of the version installed on the host, add this to jeka.properties: 

jeka.version=0.11.68

docs.title: Add dependencies
docs.text:
Your scripts can easily depend on external libraries from Maven repositories or local files.

Annotate the Script class: 

import com.github.lalyos.jfiglet.FigletFont;
import dev.jeka.core.tool.JkDep;
import dev.jeka.core.tool.JkDoc;
import dev.jeka.core.tool.KBean;

@JkDep("com.github.lalyos:jfiglet:0.0.9")
class Script extends KBean {
    // existing fields and methods
}
... and execute jeka intellij: sync to update your IDE classpath.

Now use the library in a new method: 

public void ascii() throws Exception {
    System.out.println(FigletFont.convertOneLine("Hello"));
}
... and execute jeka ascii. This library has no transitive dependency, but it could have. Try to import any library with transitive dependencies and execute jeka --inspect. This displays runtime information about the JeKa run, including the resulting classpath.

Note

JeKa also supports JBang-style dependency declarations: //DEPS com.github.lalyos:jfiglet:0.0.9

docs.title: Use BOM dependencies
docs.text:
For complex dependencies, you can import a Maven BOM:

@JkDep("com.google.cloud:libraries-bom:5.0.0@pom")
@JkDep("com.google.cloud:google-cloud-storage")
@JkDep("com.google.cloud:google-cloud-bigquery")

docs.title: File system dependencies
docs.text:
You can add local JARs or class folders:

  • Place JARs in the jeka-boot directory (create it if not present).
  • Or use @JkDep with relative paths:
@JkDep("../other-project/mylib.jar")
@JkDep("../other-project/my-classes")

docs.title: Dependencies in properties
docs.text:
Alternatively, define dependencies in jeka.properties: 

jeka.classpath=\
  com.google.cloud:libraries-bom:5.0.0@pom \
  com.google.cloud:google-cloud-storage \
  com.google.cloud:google-cloud-bigquery

docs.title: Compilation directives
docs.text:
JeKa compiles jeka-src classes on-the-fly. You can pass options to the Java compiler using @JkCompileOption:

import dev.jeka.core.tool.JkCompileOption;
import dev.jeka.core.tool.KBean;

@JkCompileOption("-Xlint:-options")
class Script extends KBean {
}

docs.title: Multi-file scripts & KBeans
docs.text:
jeka-src can host multiple scripts and utility classes. Understanding how JeKa finds and executes these classes (called KBeans) is essential.

  1. Create a new class Build.java in jeka-src: 

    import dev.jeka.core.tool.KBean;

public class Build extends KBean {
    public void foo() {
        System.out.println("Method 'foo()' is running.");
    }
}
    Execute jeka foo. It works because Build is now the default KBean: without explicit setting, this is the first one found in jeka-src, in alphabetical order (root classes first, then those in packages).

  2. Now try jeka hello. You will get an error: ERROR: Unmatched argument at index 0: 'hello'

hello is not a method of the default KBean. When multiple KBeans exist, you may need to be explicit.

  1. To execute a method from a specific KBean, use the format jeka [kbean]: [method]: jeka script: hello

  2. You can define the default KBean in jeka.properties: 

    jeka.kbean.default=script
    Now jeka hello will work again.

KBean Naming

A KBean named MyCoolKBean can be referenced as: - org.example.MyCoolKBean (Fully qualified) - MyCoolKBean (Short name) - myCoolKBean (Uncapitalized) - myCool (Omitting the 'KBean' suffix)

docs.title: Configure default values
docs.text:
You can override KBean fields directly from jeka.properties: 

@script.name=Everybody
Now jeka hello prints Hello Everybody !.

docs.title: KBean Interaction
docs.text:
KBeans can interact with each other. This is how JeKa plugins and complex build scripts are structured.

  1. Ensure jeka.kbean.default=script is set and remove the @script.name override.
  2. In Build.java, add a @JkPostInit method taking the KBean to configure as argument: 
    import dev.jeka.core.tool.JkPostInit;
import dev.jeka.core.tool.KBean;

public class Build extends KBean {

    @JkPostInit
    private void postInit(Script script) {  // the singleton instance, already initialized
        script.name = "Mates";
    }
}
  3. Execute jeka script: hello build:. Hello Mates !

The build: part in the command line forces the initialization of the build KBean, which then configures the script KBean.

To make build always initialize, add this to jeka.properties: 

@build=on

Note

@JkPostInit methods run after the command-line values have been injected, so they win: jeka hello name=Zed now prints Hello Mates !. To set a default value that can be overridden, use a static @JkPreInit method instead.

docs.title: Combine KBeans on the Command Line
docs.text:
Methods and fields belong to the KBean mentioned just before them:

jeka project: pack javaVersion=21 maven: publishLocal   # 'javaVersion' is a field of 'project'
With javaVersion=21 at the end, JeKa looks for this field in maven and fails with Unmatched argument.

docs.title: Classpath KBeans
docs.text:
Local KBeans are in jeka-src. Classpath KBeans are pre-compiled and available in the JeKa classpath (like plugins).

Run jeka --doc to see all available KBeans, including standard ones like setup. Example: jeka setup: openHomeDir

docs.title: Adding Plugins
docs.text:
Adding a plugin is as simple as adding its JAR to the classpath via jeka.classpath or @JkDep.

jeka.classpath=\
  dev.jeka:springboot-plugin  \
  dev.jeka:sonarqube-plugin \
  dev.jeka:openapi-plugin:0.11.8-1

Note

If you omit the version for dev.jeka group dependencies, JeKa uses its own version.

docs.title: Example: Running Node.js via JeKa
docs.text:
You can even add KBeans dynamically from the CLI: 

jeka -v -cp=dev.jeka:nodejs-plugin nodeJs: version="20.12.2" cmdLine="npx cowsay Hello JeKa" exec

This displays, after some logs: 

 ____________
< Hello JeKa >
 ------------
        \   ^__^
         \  (oo)\_______
            (__)\       )\/\
                ||----w |
                ||     ||
The -v (verbose) option is needed to see the output of the Node.js command.

Next steps: Learn how to Build a Base Application or a Full Project.

docs.title: Build Base-Mode
docs.text:
The codebase mode is a "best of both worlds" approach, sitting between single-file scripts like JBang and full-featured Maven or Gradle projects.

It is particularly well-suited for developing reusable JeKa plugins (KBeans), as it allows you to write your plugin code directly in jeka-src and test it immediately.

In this tutorial, we'll use the base KBean to build a Java application or library with minimal configuration.

Visit the demo-base-application repository to see a concrete example.

Tip

Run jeka base: --doc to see all available options and commands for the base KBean.

docs.title: Scaffold a New Code Base
docs.text:
To create a base structure ready for coding, run:

jeka base: scaffold scaffold.kind=APP

This generates the following project structure: 

. 
├── jeka-src             <- Source root directory
│   ├── _dev             <- Optional package containing all non-prod (build and test)
│   │   ├── test
│   │   └── Custom.java  
│   └── app              <- Suggested base package for production code/resources
│       └── App.java     
├── jeka.properties      <- Build configuration (Java and JeKa version, KBean configurations, ...)
├── jeka.ps1             <- PowerShell script to run JeKa on Windows
├── jeka                 <- Bash script to run JeKa on Linux/macOS
└── README.md            <- Describes available build commands

JeKa generates JARs, reports and other artifacts in the jeka-output directory, created on the first build.

All your Java code is supposed to be in the jeka-src folder.

_dev is a special package for source code and dependencies used only for development (e.g., tests, builds). If you're new to Java, you can ignore or delete it.

The scaffolded example includes an App class in the app package. You can add or modify classes in any package you like.

docs.title: Sync with IntelliJ
docs.text:
The easiest way to work with JeKa in IntelliJ is by using the JeKa IntelliJ Plugin. It provides syntax highlighting, auto-completion, and direct execution of JeKa commands.

To synchronize your project with IntelliJ and generate the necessary project files, run:

jeka intellij: sync

If changes don't appear or you need to re-initialize the project structure, use:

jeka intellij: initProject

docs.title: Add Dependencies
docs.text:
In base mode, dependencies are declared directly in your Java source files using the @JkDep annotation. This keeps your build configuration close to the code that uses it.

The scaffolded App.java includes an example:

jeka-src/app/App.java
@JkDep("com.github.lalyos:jfiglet:0.0.9")
public class App {
    // ...
}

For more details on how to specify dependencies, see the Dependency Management guide.

docs.title: File-based Dependencies
docs.text:
You can also include JAR files as dependencies by placing them in the jeka-boot directory. They will be automatically added to the production classpath:

├── jeka-boot      <- JARs included in the production classpath.

docs.title: Non-production Dependencies
docs.text:
Dependencies used only for development (like testing or custom build logic) should be declared in classes under the _dev package. This ensures they are not included in the final application bundle.

jeka-src/_dev/Custom.java
@JkDep("org.junit.jupiter:junit-jupiter")
@JkDep("org.junit:junit-bom:6.0.3@pom")
class Custom extends KBean {
    // ...
}

Note

Remember to run jeka intellij: sync after modifying dependencies to update your IDE's classpath.

docs.title: Run your Application
docs.text:
You can execute your application directly from the command line:

jeka -p arg0 arg1 ...  # or --program

Use the --clean (-c) option to force a clean compilation before running:

jeka -c -p

docs.title: Run from Remote Git
docs.text:
JeKa can run applications directly from a remote Git repository without having to clone it manually:

jeka --remote https://github.com/jeka-dev/demo-base-application.git -p

docs.title: Native Compilation
docs.text:
JeKa makes it easy to compile your application into a standalone native executable using GraalVM.

To compile to native, execute:

jeka native: compile

Once compiled, running jeka --program ... will automatically use the native executable instead of the JVM.

Note

If your application requires resources (like icons or config files) at runtime, you might need to set: jeka.properties

@native.includeAllResources=true

To always trigger a native build when running the application, add this to your jeka.properties:

jeka.properties
jeka.program.build=native: compile

docs.title: Dockerization
docs.text:
You can package your application into a Docker image with a single command:

jeka docker: build

This builds the image and registers it with your local Docker daemon. The console output will provide the exact command to run your new image.

To create an even smaller, faster-starting image using your native executable, run:

jeka docker: buildNative

docs.title: Pre-defined Build Commands
docs.text:
The base KBean provides several built-in commands for common tasks:

Available Base Commands
jeka base: test       # Run all tests in the _dev package
jeka base: pack       # Create application JARs (does not run tests)
jeka base: build      # Run tests, then pack
jeka base: runJar     # Execute the generated JAR
jeka base: info       # Display project configuration and dependencies
jeka base: depTree    # Display the full dependency tree

For more advanced commands, see the Project Build tutorial.

docs.title: Create a Library
docs.text:
While base mode is often used for applications, it can also be used to build and publish libraries. To do so, you must define a moduleId and a version.

Add these to your jeka.properties:

jeka.properties
@base.moduleId=org.example:my-lib
@maven.pub.version=1.0.0-SNAPSHOT

Create the JAR and publish it to a Maven repository. The JAR must exist, so run pack in the same command:

jeka base: pack maven: publish

Without a configured repository, the library is published in the JeKa local repository (~/.jeka/maven-publish-dir). See the Maven KBean to configure a remote repository.

docs.title: Building Java Projects
docs.text:
In this tutorial, we'll use the project KBean to build a Java application or library. This KBean provides build methods and a project layout similar to those of Maven and Gradle.

If you prefer a lighter structure without the standard src/main/java layout, see the Build Base tutorial.

Tip

Run jeka project: --doc to see all available options and methods.

docs.title: Scaffold a New Project
docs.text:
Run the following command to create a standard project structure, ready for coding:

jeka project: scaffold

You'll get the following project structure: 

.
├── src                  
│   ├── main
│   │   └── java         <- Java code
│   └── test
│       └── java         <- Unit tests
├── jeka-src             <- Java (or Kotlin) code for build customization
│   └── Custom.java      
├── jeka.project.deps    <- Project dependencies
├── jeka.properties      <- Build configuration and properties
├── jeka.ps1             <- PowerShell wrapper (optional)
├── jeka                 <- Bash wrapper (optional)
└── README.md            <- Project overview and build instructions

JARs, classes and reports are generated in the jeka-output directory, created on the first build.

Put resources in src/main/resources and src/test/resources.

The generated jeka.properties sets the JeKa and Java versions, makes project the default KBean, and packages the application as a FAT JAR: jeka.properties

jeka.version=0.11.68
jeka.java.version=25

jeka.kbean.default=project
@custom=on

@project.pack.jarType=FAT
@project.pack.detectMainClass=true

The jeka and jeka.ps1 scripts allow building the project on machines where JeKa is not globally installed. You can delete jeka-src/Custom.java if you don't need programmatic customization. In this case, also delete the @custom=on line.

Tip

In a directory already containing sources, use jeka project: scaffold scaffold.kind=EMPTY. It generates the same files, without sample classes. Existing files are kept. If jeka.properties or jeka.project.deps already exist, JeKa displays the lines to add.

docs.title: Simple Layout
docs.text:
If you prefer a flatter structure, scaffold the project with the SIMPLE style:

jeka project: scaffold layout.style=SIMPLE layout.mixSourcesAndResources=true

This results in a simpler layout: 

.
├── src       <- Java code and resources mixed
├── test      <- Test code and resources mixed

and adds these properties: jeka.properties

@project.layout.style=SIMPLE
@project.layout.mixSourcesAndResources=true

To convert an existing project, add these properties and move the files: src/main/java and src/main/resources to src, src/test/java and src/test/resources to test. Otherwise, the whole src directory, tests included, is compiled as production code.

docs.title: Local JAR Dependencies
docs.text:
You can also include local JARs by placing them in the libs directory:

.
├── libs                  
│   ├── compile          <- JARs for compile, runtime, and test classpaths
│   ├── compile-only     <- JARs for compile and test classpaths only
│   ├── runtime          <- JARs for runtime and test classpaths
│   └── test             <- JARs for test classpath only

docs.title: IDE Integration
docs.text:
To synchronize your project with IntelliJ IDEA, run:

jeka intellij: sync

If the project is not yet recognized as a JeKa project, use: 

jeka intellij: initProject

docs.title: Dependency Management
docs.text:
Dependencies are declared in jeka.project.deps. JeKa supports Maven coordinates and BOMs.

jeka.project.deps
[version]    # Define versions or import BOMs
org.junit:junit-bom:5.12.2@pom

[compile]    # Main dependencies
com.google.guava:guava:33.4.0-jre
com.google.code.gson:gson:2.13.1

[compile-only] # Only needed for compilation (e.g., Lombok)
org.projectlombok:lombok:1.18.38

[runtime]    # Only needed at runtime
org.postgresql:postgresql:42.7.4

[test]       # Only needed for testing
org.junit.jupiter:junit-jupiter
org.junit.platform:junit-platform-launcher

[processor]  # Annotation processors
org.projectlombok:lombok:1.18.38
Section Description [version] Versions and BOM imports (using @pom). [compile] Included in compile, runtime, and test classpaths. [compile-only] Included in compile and test, but NOT runtime. [runtime] Included in runtime and test, but NOT compile. [test] Included in the test classpath only. [processor] Annotation processors. Not included in any classpath. See Annotation Processors.

You can also reference local files: libs/my-local-lib.jar.

docs.title: Java Version
docs.text:
By default, the project targets the Java version running JeKa, set by jeka.java.version in jeka.properties. JeKa itself needs Java 21 or higher. To target another version, set:

jeka.properties
@project.javaVersion=21

Note

By default, tests run in a forked process, on a JDK of the target version. This does not work yet for targets below 21: project: test fails with UnsupportedClassVersionError. For such targets, run the tests in the JeKa process: jeka.properties

@project.javaVersion=17
@project.test.fork=false
Classes are then compiled for Java 17, and tests run on the JDK running JeKa.

docs.title: Run Tests
docs.text:
jeka project: test                                          # all tests
jeka project: test test.includePatterns='.*MainTest'        # a single test class
jeka project: test test.includePatterns='com.acme.Order.*'  # several test classes
jeka project: build -Djeka.test.skip=true                   # full build, without tests

test.includePatterns is a space-separated list of regular expressions, matching fully qualified class names. Quote it, as some shells expand *.

docs.title: JAR Packaging
docs.text:
The scaffolded jeka.properties sets a FAT JAR. Without this property, JeKa creates a regular JAR.

jeka.properties
@project.pack.jarType=FAT
Type Description REGULAR (default) Contains the project classes and resources only. FAT Includes all runtime dependencies. SHADE Same as FAT, with the dependency packages relocated.

Note

SHADE relocates classes and META-INF/services files, but not the class names written in other text files. For example, logback.xml must mention the relocated name: my.app._shaded.ch.qos.logback.core.ConsoleAppender, where my.app is the root package of your application. Prefer FAT for applications that don't need relocation.

Frameworks that list classes in their own resource files, such as Micronaut (META-INF/micronaut/...), don't start from a shaded jar: use FAT for them.

docs.title: Multiple Artifacts
docs.text:
For libraries, you might want to produce both a regular JAR and an extra shaded JAR:

jeka.properties
# Main JAR without dependencies
@project.pack.jarType=REGULAR

# Produce an extra shaded jar suffixed with '-all'
@project.pack.shadeJarClassifier=all

# Ensure the extra artifact is published to Maven
@maven.pub.extraArtifacts=all

docs.title: Versioning and Git
docs.text:
You can hardcode the version in jeka.properties:

jeka.properties
@project.moduleId=com.example:my-app
@project.version=1.0.0-SNAPSHOT

docs.title: Automatic Git Versioning
docs.text:
The recommended approach is to let JeKa infer the version from Git:

jeka.properties
@project.gitVersioning.enable=true

The project must be in a Git repository having at least one commit. Otherwise, commands fail with a bare Git error (code 128 or 129).

  • If you are on a Tag: The version is the tag name (e.g., 1.2.3).
  • If you are on a Branch: The version is [branch]-SNAPSHOT (e.g., master-SNAPSHOT), with / replaced by - (feat/x gives feat-x-SNAPSHOT).
  • Metadata: The JAR manifest will automatically include Git commit ID, branch, and "dirty" state.

docs.title: Common Flags
docs.text:
• -c or --clean: Deletes jeka-output before running.
  • -v or --verbose: Shows detailed logs.
  • -p or --program: Runs the generated application.

docs.title: Project Lifecycle
docs.text: Command Description jeka project: compile Compiles source code. jeka project: test Runs unit tests (e.g., JUnit). jeka project: pack Packages the project into a JAR. jeka project: build Full cycle: clean, compile, test, pack, quality checks, end-to-end tests. jeka project: runJar Executes the generated JAR. jeka project: info Displays project setup and properties. jeka project: depTree Prints the full dependency tree.

docs.title: Extensions (Optional)
docs.text:
• jeka native: compile: Compiles to a GraalVM native executable.
  • jeka docker: build: Creates a Docker image.
  • jeka project: pack maven: publishLocal: Publishes to the JeKa local repository. See Maven KBean.

docs.title: Quality & Coverage (Plugins)
docs.text:
JeKa plugins like JaCoCo and SonarQube can be added via jeka.properties.

jeka.properties
# Inject plugins into the build classpath
jeka.classpath=dev.jeka:sonarqube-plugin dev.jeka:jacoco-plugin

# Activate JaCoCo for the project
@jacoco=on

# Configure SonarQube
sonar.host.url=http://localhost:9000

# Create a shortcut command for full build + quality check
jeka.cmd.quality=project: test pack sonarqube: run

Run with: jeka ::quality.

docs.title: Programmatic Customization
docs.text:
For complex logic, use jeka-src/Custom.java. This allows you to hook into the build lifecycle using @JkPostInit.

jeka-src/Custom.java
import dev.jeka.core.tool.JkDoc;
import dev.jeka.core.tool.KBean;
import dev.jeka.core.tool.builtins.project.ProjectKBean;
import dev.jeka.core.tool.JkPostInit;

public class Custom extends KBean {

    @JkPostInit(required = true)
    private void postInit(ProjectKBean projectKBean) {
        // Customize compiler options
        projectKBean.project.compilation.addJavaCompilerOptions("-Xlint:unchecked");

        // Add a runtime dependency
        projectKBean.project.pack.runtimeDependencies.add("org.postgresql:postgresql:42.7.4");
    }

    @JkDoc("Custom action that can be called from CLI")
    public void myAction() {
        System.out.println("Hello from Custom KBean!");
    }
}

Run your custom action with: jeka custom: myAction.

Note

The JkProject object is the heart of the project KBean. It provides a rich API for every aspect of the build. See API Reference.

docs.title: Migrate a Maven Project
docs.text:
This tutorial converts an existing single-module Maven project to JeKa. Sources stay in place, as JeKa uses the same src/main/java and src/test/java layout by default. The pom.xml file is kept until you are satisfied with the result.

You need the JeKa CLI, and Maven (mvn in the PATH, or a mvnw wrapper in the project).

docs.title: 1. Generate the JeKa Files
docs.text:
Commit your work first, then execute from the directory containing the pom.xml file:

jeka project: scaffold scaffold.kind=EMPTY

This adds jeka.properties, jeka.project.deps, and the jeka and jeka.ps1 wrapper scripts. kind=EMPTY avoids generating the sample classes. Existing files, as README.md, are kept.

docs.title: 2. Convert the Dependencies
docs.text:
jeka maven: migrateDeps

This displays the dependencies of the pom.xml as Java code, then as jeka.project.deps content. Copy the latter into jeka.project.deps, replacing its content:

jeka.project.deps
[compile]
com.google.guava:guava:33.4.8-jre

[compile-only]
org.projectlombok:lombok:1.18.38

[runtime]
org.postgresql:postgresql:42.7.4

[test]
org.junit.jupiter:junit-jupiter:5.12.2

If lombok or another dependency is an annotation processor, also declare it in a [processor] section:

[processor]
org.projectlombok:lombok:1.18.38

Maven scopes translate as follows:

Maven jeka.project.deps compile [compile] provided [compile-only] runtime [runtime] test [test] <annotationProcessorPaths> [processor] <dependencyManagement>, import scope [version], with @pom suffix for BOMs <exclusions> !group:name lines, below the dependency

The system scope translates to file paths in [compile-only]. Annotation processors are not translated.

Check these cases by hand:

  • Dependencies with a classifier do not bring their transitive dependencies in JeKa. A comment is displayed next to them.
  • Dependencies of type pom are displayed as comments. Declare the dependencies they bring instead.
  • An external parent POM managing versions is declared as a BOM in [version].
  • Versions managed in Maven profiles are not added to [version].

See jeka.project.deps for the complete syntax.

docs.title: 3. Set the Coordinates and the Java Version
docs.text:
Replace the content of jeka.properties, keeping the generated jeka.version:

jeka.properties
jeka.version=0.11.68
jeka.java.version=21
jeka.kbean.default=project

@project=on
@project.moduleId=com.acme:shop
@project.version=1.0.0
Maven JeKa groupId, artifactId @project.moduleId=com.acme:shop version @project.version=1.0.0, or @project.gitVersioning.enable=true maven.compiler.release jeka.java.version (21 or higher) or @project.javaVersion <compilerArgs> @project.compilation.compilerOptions=-Xlint:unchecked <mainClass> of the JAR or Shade plugin @project.pack.mainClass, or @project.pack.detectMainClass=true Shade or Assembly plugin @project.pack.jarType=FAT (or SHADE to relocate packages) Repositories of settings.xml jeka.repos.download Other plugins KBeans, in jeka-src or from a plugin JAR

For a target lower than Java 21, see Java Version.

docs.title: 4. Build and Compare
docs.text:
jeka project: test pack --clean

Then check that the result matches the Maven build:

jeka project: depTree     # compare with 'mvn dependency:tree'
jeka project: info        # versions, source locations, main class...
jeka maven: info          # what will be published

In IntelliJ, execute jeka intellij: sync to use the JeKa dependencies. When done, delete the pom.xml file and the Maven wrapper.

docs.title: Command Equivalents
docs.text: See Common Commands.

docs.title: Multi-Module Projects
docs.text:
Repeat the steps above in each module, then:

  • Declare the modules in the jeka.properties of the parent directory: _jeka.child-bases=core, plugins/*.
  • Replace dependencies between modules by relative paths in jeka.project.deps, as ../core.
  • Move the content of <dependencyManagement> to the [version] section of the jeka.project.deps of the parent directory.

See Multi-Module.

Note

For now, dependencies on sibling modules are missing from the published POM.

docs.title: Keep Building with Maven
docs.text: JeKa can also run an existing Maven build, for instance to make the application runnable from Git. See Run Maven.

docs.title: Source-Runnable Applications
docs.text: With JeKa, distributing software doesn't require creating and publishing binaries. JeKa acts as a source-based application manager, letting you run programs directly from their remote Git repository or install them on a user's machine by building them at installation time.

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
To run an application directly from its Git repository, use the following command:

jeka --remote GIT_URL --program PROGRAM_ARGUMENTS
or 
jeka -r GIT_URL -p PROGRAM_ARGUMENTS

Example: 

jeka -r https://github.com/jeka-dev/demo-cowsay -p "Hello JeKa!"
You can pass -Dxxxxx=yyyy as a program argument to set system properties.

The first run clones and builds the application, with the JeKa and Java versions set in the jeka.properties of the repository. They are downloaded if needed, and may differ from those installed on your machine.

docs.title: Browsing the Catalog
docs.text:
You can see a list of available application catalogs by executing: 

jeka app: catalog

To see applications within a specific catalog: 

jeka app: catalog name=demo
This will list the application names, descriptions, and commands to run or install them.

docs.title: Running Specific Versions
docs.text:
You can run a specific version of an application by appending a tag name to the URL:

jeka -r https://github.com/jeka-dev/demo-cowsay#0.0.6 -p "Hello JeKa!"

docs.title: Trust and Security
docs.text:
Only run applications from sources you trust, as they execute code on your machine. Repositories from github.com/jeka-dev/ are trusted by default.

When using another repository with jeka -r (with or without -p) or jeka app: install, JeKa asks you to confirm that you trust the URL, before cloning it. If you accept, the URL is added to the trusted list.

Without a terminal (CI, scripts), JeKa cannot ask: jeka -r stops with exit code 1. Declare the trusted URLs beforehand.

There are several ways to trust a URL:

  • Accept it when JeKa asks.
  • Add it with jeka app: trustUrl url=github.com/djeang/kill8.
  • Edit [JEKA_USER_HOME]/global.properties (~/.jeka/global.properties by default), using a space-separated list: 
    jeka.app.url.trusted=github.com/djeang/kill8 github.com/my-org/
  • Set the JEKA_APP_URL_TRUSTED environment variable, in the same format. It replaces the list of global.properties for jeka -r, but is not used by app: install.

Tip

Prefer entries naming a single repository (github.com/djeang/kill8). To trust all the repositories of an account, use github.com/my-org/.

docs.title: Native Executables
docs.text:
To improve startup performance, you can compile a remote application to a native executable. Once compiled, all subsequent runs will use the native version.

jeka -r https://github.com/jeka-dev/demo-cowsay#0.0.9 native: compile

docs.title: Command Shorthands
docs.text:
Typing and remembering full repository URLs can be tedious. You can simplify this by using shortcuts in your ~/.jeka/global.properties file:

jeka.cmd.cowsay=-r https://github.com/jeka-dev/demo-cowsay#0.0.9 -p
Now you can invoke the application using the :: prefix: 
jeka ::cowsay "Hello World!"

docs.title: Desktop Installation
docs.text:
JeKa lets you install applications for direct execution from your terminal, making them available in your system PATH.

Add ~/.jeka/apps to your PATH first. Otherwise, applications are installed in the JeKa distribution directory, and may be lost when switching versions (e.g. with SDKMAN!).

jeka app: install repo=https://github.com/djeang/kill8
JeKa may ask for:

  • Confirmation, if the URL is not trusted.
  • The version, if the repository has tags: press Enter for the proposed tag, type another tag, or @ for the last commit.
  • The name of the application, unless set with name=... or if installed from a catalog.

These questions need a terminal: without it, the command fails. The #tag suffix is for jeka -r only, not for repo=.

Or use a shorthand for applications listed in a catalog: 

jeka app: install repo=kill8@djeang

For faster startup, you can install the native version (requires GraalVM): 

jeka app: install repo=kill8@djeang runtime=NATIVE

Once installed, you can simply call the application by name: 

kill8 8081

docs.title: Managing Installed Applications
docs.text:
To list all applications installed on your system via JeKa: 

jeka app: list

To update an application to its latest version (highest semantic tag or latest commit): 

jeka app: update name=kill8

To remove an application from your system: 

jeka app: uninstall name=kill8

docs.title: Desktop GUI Applications
docs.text:
If the application is a GUI, you can install it as a standalone desktop application. 

jeka app: install repo=kill8@djeang runtime=BUNDLE
This will create a .dmg (macOS) or .exe (Windows) installer that you can use to install the application on your desktop.

For more details on application management, see the App KBean Reference.

docs.title: JeKa Projects
docs.text:
Applications built with JeKa are "source-runnable" by default.

When running or installing a remote application, JeKa clones the repository and builds it:

  1. It tries to execute the command specified in the jeka.program.build property from the project's jeka.properties.
  2. If this property is missing, it runs jeka project: pack pack.jarType=FAT pack.detectMainClass=true -Djeka.test.skip=true (for Java projects with a src directory).
  3. Otherwise, it runs jeka base: pack -Djeka.test.skip=true.

For native execution (or when runtime=NATIVE), JeKa:

  1. Tries to execute the command specified in jeka.program.build.native.
  2. If missing, it uses jeka.program.build followed by native: compile.
  3. If both are missing, it runs native: compile.

JeKa then looks in the jeka-output directory to run the resulting JAR or native binary.

docs.title: Maven Projects
docs.text:
Maven projects can be installed from source using the maven: KBean. Add a jeka.properties file to your Maven project root to configure the build delegation:

jeka.java.version=21

# Delegate build to Maven wrapper
jeka.program.build=maven: wrapPackage

# Optional: use this for native builds. Set the GraalVM version used to build the native executable.
jeka.program.build.native=maven: wrapPackage args="-Pnative" -Djeka.java.distrib=graalvm -Djeka.java.version=25

For multi-module projects, specify which module contains the application: 

jeka.program.build=maven: wrapPackage appModule=app

For desktop applications (installed using runtime=BUNDLE), specify the Maven command and the location of the distribution: 

jeka.program.build.bundle=maven: wrapPackage args="-Pjpackage"
jeka.program.bundle.dist=target/dist

Requirements:

  1. Maven wrapper (recommended): Include mvnw / mvnw.cmd in your repository, to make the build fully portable. Otherwise, mvn must be in the PATH.
  2. Fat JAR plugin: Configure maven-shade-plugin to create an executable JAR, with a main class. Otherwise, running the application fails with no main manifest attribute. 
    <plugin>
  <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
  <artifactId>maven-shade-plugin</artifactId>
  <version>3.6.0</version>
  <executions>
    <execution>
      <phase>package</phase>
      <goals><goal>shade</goal></goals>
      <configuration>
        <transformers>
          <transformer implementation="org.apache.maven.plugins.shade.resource.ManifestResourceTransformer">
            <mainClass>com.example.app.App</mainClass>
          </transformer>
        </transformers>
      </configuration>
    </execution>
  </executions>
</plugin>
  3. Native support (optional): Add native-maven-plugin in a Maven profile.

See a complete example at demo-maven-multimodule.

docs.title: Gradle Projects
docs.text:
Gradle projects can be made source-runnable using the gradle: KBean from the Gradle plugin.

Add a jeka.properties file to your Gradle project root:

jeka.java.version=21

jeka.classpath=dev.jeka:gradle-plugin
jeka.program.build=gradle: wrapBuild

For multi-module projects, specify which sub-module contains the application: 

jeka.program.build=gradle: wrapBuild appModule=app

For native execution (requires GraalVM), add jeka.program.build.native: 

jeka.program.build.native=gradle: wrapNative appModule=app -Djeka.java.distrib=graalvm -Djeka.java.version=21

Requirements:

  1. Gradle wrapper: Include gradlew / gradlew.bat in your repository (to make the build fully portable).
  2. Fat JAR: Configure the jar task to produce an executable fat JAR with Main-Class in the manifest:
jar {
    manifest {
        attributes 'Main-Class': 'com.example.app.App'
    }
    from {
        configurations.runtimeClasspath.collect { it.isDirectory() ? it : zipTree(it) }
    }
    duplicatesStrategy = DuplicatesStrategy.EXCLUDE
}
  1. Native support (optional): Add the GraalVM Native Build Tools plugin in the application module:
plugins {
    id 'org.graalvm.buildtools.native' version '0.10.3'
}

See a complete example at plugins/plugins.gradle/sample.

docs.title: Custom Build Commands
docs.text:
For other build tools or custom requirements, you can create a custom KBean to handle the build process:

jeka.program.build=custom: build
jeka.program.build.native=custom: buildNative

import dev.jeka.core.api.file.JkPathTree;
import dev.jeka.core.api.system.JkLocator;
import dev.jeka.core.api.system.JkLog;
import dev.jeka.core.api.system.JkProcess;
import dev.jeka.core.tool.JkConstants;
import dev.jeka.core.tool.JkDoc;
import dev.jeka.core.tool.KBean;

import java.io.File;
import java.nio.file.Files;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.nio.file.StandardCopyOption;

class Custom extends KBean {

    @JkDoc("Build application and copy result to jeka-output")
    public void build() {
        gradle("clean assemble");
        copyToJekaOutput();
    }

    @JkDoc("Build native application")
    public void buildNative() {
        gradle("clean nativeCompile");
        copyToJekaOutput();
    }

    private void gradle(String gradleArguments) {
        JkLog.info("Executing gradlew " + gradleArguments);
        String distrib = getRunbase().getProperties().get("jeka.java.distrib", "graalvm");
        String javaVersion = getRunbase().getProperties().get("jeka.java.version", "21");
        String distribFolder = distrib + "-" + javaVersion;
        Path graalvmHome = JkLocator.getCacheDir().resolve("jdks").resolve(distribFolder);
        String newPath = graalvmHome.resolve("bin") + File.pathSeparator + System.getenv("PATH");
        JkProcess.ofWinOrUx("gradlew.bat", "./gradlew")
                .addParamsAsCmdLine(gradleArguments)
                .setWorkingDir(getBaseDir())
                .setEnv("JAVA_HOME", graalvmHome.toString())
                .setEnv("GRAALVM_HOME", graalvmHome.toString())
                .setEnv("PATH", newPath)
                .setInheritIO(true)
                .exec();
    }

    private void copyToJekaOutput() {
        JkPathTree.of(getBaseDir().resolve("build/libs"))
                .andMatching("*.jar")
                .copyTo(getBaseDir().resolve(JkConstants.OUTPUT_PATH),
                        StandardCopyOption.REPLACE_EXISTING);
        Path nativeDir = getBaseDir().resolve("build/native/nativeCompile");
        if (Files.exists(nativeDir)) {
            JkPathTree.of(nativeDir).copyTo(getBaseDir().resolve(JkConstants.OUTPUT_PATH),
                        StandardCopyOption.REPLACE_EXISTING);
        }
    }
}

docs.title: Docker Integration
docs.text:

Create a JVM image: 

jeka -r https://github.com/jeka-dev/demo-cowsay docker: build

Create a native image: 

jeka -r https://github.com/jeka-dev/demo-cowsay docker: buildNative
